text: CHAPTER 2 Risk Factors Common in Student Life Risk factors are conditions or experiences that, across many students, are associated with a higher probability of depression or anxiety. Knowing them is not the same as predicting your future — but it tells you where to look. SAFETY NOTE Risk factors are statistical associations, not predictions. Having several risk factors does not mean you will develop depression or anxiety. Having none does not guarantee you will not. Use this chapter to understand the landscape, not to label yourself. A useful way to think about risk factors is to borrow an image from public health. Imagine depression and anxiety as a fire. A fire needs fuel, oxygen, and a spark. Risk factors are the fuel — they make a fire more likely and, when it starts, more intense. Protective factors, covered in Chapter 3, are the firebreaks — they make a fire less likely to start and easier to contain if it does. None of this is deterministic. People with many risk factors never develop a condition; people with few sometimes do. But on average, across populations, the pattern is clear: more risk factors, fewer protective factors, more depression and anxiety. Student life amplifies several risk factors in particular ways. The transition from a structured family environment to a largely self-structured academic environment, often combined with a new city, new social network, new financial responsibilities, and the developmental task of forming an adult identity, creates a perfect storm of fuel.

This chapter walks through the most consistent and wellstudied risk factors in the student mental-health literature, what each one looks like in daily life, and a preview of "what helps" — the practices and conditions that, according to the research, can blunt the effect of each risk factor. The detailed practices themselves are covered in Chapters 4 to 12. 2.1 Loneliness and social isolation Loneliness is the single most consistent psychosocial predictor of depression in the student literature. It is also one of the most under-acknowledged. There is a cultural narrative that university is automatically a social, vibrant time of life, and students who feel lonely often conclude that there is something uniquely wrong with them. The data say otherwise: in the Healthy Minds Study, the largest annual survey of student mental health in the United States, more than half of students report moderate to severe loneliness, and the figure has been rising for over a decade.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: It is important to distinguish being alone from feeling lonely. Being alone is a state — and many students genuinely enjoy and need solitude. Feeling lonely is a subjective experience of the gap between the social connection you want and the social connection you have. You can feel lonely in a crowded lecture hall, at a party, or in a relationship. You can also be alone for a weekend and feel perfectly content. Loneliness is not about the number of people around you; it is about the perceived quality and depth of your connection to them. Loneliness raises depression risk through several mechanisms. Acutely, it activates the same threat-detection circuits in the brain that respond to physical pain — humans are social primates, and isolation registers as danger. Chronically, it elevates cortisol (the body's main stress hormone), disrupts sleep, increases systemic inflammation, and reduces the practice of emotion regulation that comes from talking through problems with trusted others. Lonely students ruminate more, sleep worse, and recover more slowly from setbacks. WHAT HELPS (PREVIEW — FULL CHAPTER IN CHAPTER 6) Loneliness is one of the most modifiable risk factors in this list. Belonging can be built. The evidence-based moves are: small repeated contact with the same people (clubs, study groups, part-time work), depth over breadth in friendships, explicit disclosure (vulnerability invites vulnerability), peersupport programmes, and reducing the comparison-and-withdrawal cycle driven by social media. See Chapter 6 for the full picture. 2.2 Academic stress and perfectionism Academic stress is the most universal student risk factor — universal because it is built into the structure of higher education.

See Chapter 6 for the full picture. 2.2 Academic stress and perfectionism Academic stress is the most universal student risk factor — universal because it is built into the structure of higher education. Deadlines, exams, grades, comparisons to peers, and the perceived link between academic outcome and life trajectory are constant sources of activation for the stress-response system. Not all academic stress is harmful; the right amount, with the right recovery, can sharpen performance and build resilience. The problem is that modern student life rarely allows sufficient recovery. Back-to-back deadlines, the encroachment of academic work into evenings and weekends, and the "always available" expectation created by email and learning-management systems mean that the body's stress response is activated for weeks or months without the dips that allow it to reset.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Within academic stress, perfectionism deserves special attention. Perfectionism is not the same as having high standards. It is the belief that anything less than flawless is failure, combined with harsh self-criticism when perfection is (inevitably) not achieved. Perfectionism is strongly and specifically associated with anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and burnout in students. It is also socially rewarded — universities select for it, employers reward it, and families praise it — which makes it easy to mistake for a virtue rather than a vulnerability. A closely related pattern is maladaptive procrastination, which is not laziness but an anxiety-driven avoidance response. The perfectionist student does not put off work because they do not care; they put it off because starting it confronts them with the possibility of not doing it perfectly. The avoidance provides shortterm relief and long-term catastrophe — late, rushed, lower-quality work, combined with days or weeks of dread. Understanding this loop is the first step out of it. WHAT HELPS (PREVIEW — FULL CHAPTER IN CHAPTER 7) Time management that respects energy, not just hours. Realistic standards ("good enough" is often the optimal standard). Breaking large tasks into the smallest possible first step. Self-compassion practices that interrupt the perfectionism–procrastination loop. Honest conversations with advisors about workload. Use of accommodations when needed. See Chapter 7. 2.3 Financial stress and food insecurity Financial stress is one of the most under-discussed risk factors in student mental health, in part because money is a particularly shame-laden topic in many cultures. Students who are struggling financially often hide it from peers, which deepens isolation and prevents access to support.

Students who are struggling financially often hide it from peers, which deepens isolation and prevents access to support. The Healthy Minds Study and parallel research in Europe, Asia, and Latin America consistently find that financial stress is one of the strongest predictors of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation in students — stronger, in many studies, than academic stress. A particularly severe form is food insecurity, defined as limited or uncertain availability of nutritionally adequate and safe food. Surveys in the United States and elsewhere find that between 20 and 40 percent of students at four-year institutions experience some level of food insecurity in a given year. Food

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: insecurity is associated with depression, anxiety, lower GPA, and higher rates of dropout. It is not a "lifestyle" issue; it is a basic-needs failure with direct mentalhealth consequences. Financial stress raises depression risk through several pathways. Directly, it chronically activates the stress response and limits access to the very things that would protect mental health (nutritious food, stable housing, time for sleep and exercise, social activities that cost money, mental-health care). Indirectly, it forces students into long work hours that compete with sleep, study, and social connection, and it produces a constant low-grade cognitive load — the mental bandwidth consumed by tracking expenses, deciding what to skip, and planning around shortfalls. This cognitive load is itself exhausting and is sometimes called "scarcity mindset": the brain, preoccupied with immediate deficits, loses capacity for longer-term planning and enjoyment. WHAT HELPS (PREVIEW — FULL CHAPTER IN CHAPTER 8) Knowing what support exists and how to access it: campus food pantries, emergency aid funds, government benefits you may be eligible for, fee waivers, scholarships, and basic-needs navigation services. Reducing shame by talking to a trusted advisor. Budgeting practices that reduce cognitive load rather than increase it. See Chapter 8. 2.4 Sleep disruption If you read only one section of this chapter, read this one. Sleep disruption is the single most biologically direct risk factor for both depression and anxiety in students. It is also, conveniently, one of the most modifiable. Sleep is not "recovery from life"; it is an active neurological process during which the brain consolidates memory, regulates emotion, clears metabolic waste, and recalibrates the stress-response system.

Sleep is not "recovery from life"; it is an active neurological process during which the brain consolidates memory, regulates emotion, clears metabolic waste, and recalibrates the stress-response system. When sleep is short, fragmented, or mistimed, every one of those processes degrades — and mood, attention, and resilience degrade with them. Students are uniquely vulnerable to sleep disruption. The transition to university often means the loss of parental sleep structure; later class times; the social pull of late-night activities; the use of screens, often in bed, late into the night; the biologically driven shift in circadian rhythm that occurs in late adolescence and pushes bedtimes later; and the consumption of caffeine, alcohol, and other

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: substances that fragment sleep. The result, in many student populations, is an average sleep duration of six hours or less on weekdays — about 90 minutes short of the seven to nine hours most young adults need. Chronically short sleep does not just make you tired. It produces measurable changes in the brain's amygdala (the structure that processes threat), making it roughly 60 percent more reactive to negative stimuli. It reduces prefrontal cortex activity, weakening the executive control that normally keeps the amygdala in check. It impairs the consolidation of positive emotional memories while sparing negative ones — meaning that, over time, sleep-deprived students remember the bad parts of their week and forget the good. It dysregulates appetite hormones, increasing cravings for high-sugar, high-fat foods. It raises inflammation and cortisol. And it directly worsens symptoms of both depression and anxiety. WHAT HELPS (PREVIEW — FULL CHAPTER IN CHAPTER 4) A consistent wake time (more important than a consistent bedtime). Morning light exposure. Screens off or shifted to warm/dim modes in the hour before bed. Caffeine cutoff in early afternoon. Treating sleep as nonnegotiable protected time, not as the flexible part of your schedule. See Chapter 4. 2.5 Identity-based stress and discrimination For students who belong to one or more marginalised groups — by race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, disability, religion, immigration status, or social class — the standard risk factors above are compounded by identity-based stress.

This includes overt experiences of discrimination and harassment; subtler but persistent microaggressions; the cognitive load of code-switching (adjusting your speech, behaviour, or appearance to fit the dominant culture); the experience of being a "token" representative of your group in classrooms or social settings; and the constant low-level question of whether a given interaction or outcome was shaped by bias. Identity-based stress is not just additive; it is multiplicative. A first-generation student of colour who is also LGBTQ+ and financially stressed is not experiencing four separate risk factors — they are experiencing a single, interlocking system of stressors that shape every aspect of university life. The mental-health impact is well-documented: students from marginalised groups show higher rates of depression and anxiety, lower rates of formal help-seeking,

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: and higher rates of negative experiences when they do seek help. This is not a deficiency in the students. It is a deficiency in the environments they are navigating. It is worth naming one specific form of identity-based stress that is often invisible to those who do not experience it: minority stress, the chronic excess stress that results from being a member of a stigmatised group, independent of any single discriminatory event. Minority stress explains why, even in the absence of overt discrimination on a given day, students from marginalised groups can show measurable physiological activation (elevated cortisol, restless sleep) that their peers do not. It is the weather, not the storm. WHAT HELPS (PREVIEW — FULL CHAPTER IN CHAPTER 12) Finding community with others who share your identity. Seeking out culturally responsive counsellors or peer supporters. Naming microaggressions when you have the energy to. Identifying allies who will do the naming for you when you do not. Recognising that the problem is the environment, not your reaction to it. See Chapter 12. 2.6 Transition stress Every transition — even a wanted one — is stressful. The first year of university is one of the largest transitions in modern life: new city, new housing, new social network, new academic expectations, new financial responsibilities, new food, new sleep schedule, new identity. The brain handles novelty well in small doses and poorly in avalanches, and the first term of university is an avalanche. The same is true, to a lesser extent, of returning after a break or a leave of absence, transferring institutions, studying abroad, and graduating. Transition stress is often misread by students as personal failure.

The same is true, to a lesser extent, of returning after a break or a leave of absence, transferring institutions, studying abroad, and graduating. Transition stress is often misread by students as personal failure. "I should be enjoying this." "Everyone else is having the time of their life." The reality is that adjustment to a major transition takes six to twelve weeks for most students, and the dip in mood and increase in anxiety during the first weeks is normal, not pathological. The risk arises when the dip does not lift, when it deepens into withdrawal, or when it interacts with pre-existing vulnerabilities — a student with a history of depression is at higher risk of relapse during a transition, and a student with no history may experience their first depressive episode during one.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: WHAT HELPS (PREVIEW — FULL CHAPTER IN CHAPTER 11) Setting realistic expectations for the transition period. Keeping anchors from before the transition (a friend from home, a familiar routine, a hobby). Building structure into the first weeks. Avoiding the "everyone else is fine" comparison by talking honestly with peers. See Chapter 11. 2.7 Substance use Substance use occupies an awkward place in student mental health. Alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, and (increasingly) prescription stimulants are woven into the social fabric of many universities, and the line between use and misuse is often blurred. The relationship between substance use and depression or anxiety runs in both directions: students who are depressed or anxious often self-medicate with substances, and substance use itself can cause or worsen depression and anxiety. Untangling the two is a job for a clinician; what this guide can do is describe the patterns and their risks. Alcohol is the most common. It is a central nervous system depressant — meaning it literally depresses neural activity — and while it produces short-term relaxation and disinhibition, it disrupts sleep architecture, worsens mood over the following days, and interacts dangerously with many antidepressant medications. Binge drinking (typically defined as five or more drinks in a single occasion for men, four or more for women) is associated with markedly higher rates of depression, anxiety, academic problems, and sexual assault in student populations. Cannabis occupies a more contested space. For some students, occasional use produces relaxation and social enjoyment without obvious harm.

Cannabis occupies a more contested space. For some students, occasional use produces relaxation and social enjoyment without obvious harm. For others — particularly those with a personal or family history of psychosis, and particularly with high-THC products — cannabis use is associated with increased anxiety, panic attacks, motivational syndrome, and, in vulnerable individuals, the onset of psychotic symptoms. The relationship with depression is more ambiguous but appears to be dose-dependent: heavy daily use is consistently associated with worse outcomes; occasional use is harder to distinguish from no effect. Prescription stimulants (used without a prescription, or above prescribed doses) are common in academic environments as "study aids". They produce shortterm focus but disrupt sleep, raise anxiety, and produce rebound fatigue that worsens the next day's performance. Their use as cognitive enhancers is also associated with higher rates of anxiety disorders in the medium term.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: WHAT HELPS Tracking your own use honestly. Noticing whether substances are being used for fun (often fine) or to cope with distress (often a warning sign). Talking to a counsellor or doctor if you are concerned. Avoiding mixing substances. Following low-risk drinking guidelines if you choose to drink. Recognising that "everyone does it" is not the same as "this is working for me". 2.8 Childhood adversity and trauma history Students who experienced significant adversity in childhood — abuse, neglect, household dysfunction, parental mental illness or substance use, loss of a parent, bullying, or exposure to violence — are at substantially elevated risk for depression, anxiety, and several other mental health conditions during the university years. The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) literature has documented a strong dose-response relationship between the number of childhood adversities and adult risk of mental and physical health conditions. This does not mean adversity is destiny. It means it changes the baseline. Trauma-informed care has become the standard framework in university counselling services, and most services now screen for trauma history and adjust their approach accordingly. If you have a trauma history, you may find that certain experiences in university — a romantic breakup, a difficult roommate situation, a medical procedure, a classroom discussion of sensitive material — produce reactions that feel out of proportion to the current event. This is not weakness. It is the nervous system recognising a pattern. Skilled support can help you distinguish past from present and build capacity to stay regulated in triggering situations. WHAT HELPS Working with a trauma-informed therapist (most university counselling services can refer you).

text: 2.9 Family history and genetic vulnerability Depression and anxiety run in families, partly through shared environment and partly through genetic influence. Having a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) with major depression roughly doubles your lifetime risk; for anxiety disorders the increase is similar. This is not a gene "for" depression; it is a set of many genetic variants, each with small effect, that collectively shape temperamental traits like neuroticism (sensitivity to negative emotion) and stress reactivity. Knowing your family history is useful, not because it dooms you, but because it informs how seriously to take early warning signs. If you have a strong family history and you notice persistent low mood, it is reasonable to seek support sooner rather than later. The same applies to other conditions that travel with depression and anxiety: bipolar disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, eating disorders, substance use disorders, and psychotic disorders. Family history is one piece of information among many — but it is a piece worth knowing. 2.10 The interaction effect: why risk factors multiply rather than add The most important thing to understand about risk factors is that they do not simply add up. They interact. A student who is sleep-deprived, lonely, financially stressed, and socially anxious is not four times as likely to develop depression as a student with none of those factors — they are many times more likely, because each factor makes the others worse. Sleep deprivation worsens social anxiety. Financial stress worsens sleep. Loneliness amplifies the cognitive impact of sleep deprivation. And so on. This is the bad news. The good news, which we will return to repeatedly, is that the same interaction effect works in reverse.

text: The next chapter turns to the other half of the picture: the protective factors that, across many studies, are associated with lower risk of depression and anxiety, and with faster recovery when they do occur. CHAPTER 3 Protective Factors and Sources of Strength If risk factors are the fuel, protective factors are the firebreaks. They do not guarantee you will never struggle — but they make struggling less likely, less severe, and shorter when it happens. SAFETY NOTE Protective factors are not a "cure" for depression or anxiety. They support mental health in general. If you are currently experiencing significant symptoms, please see Chapter 13 — protective practices and professional support work together, not instead of each other. Protective factors are the mirror image of risk factors. Where risk factors raise the probability of depression or anxiety across a population, protective factors lower it. They do so through three broad mechanisms. Some buffer — they reduce the impact of stress when it arrives, like shock absorbers on a car. Some build — they increase your baseline capacity, like strengthening a muscle so it is less likely to tear under load. Some restore — they help you return to baseline after a stressor, like sleep after a hard day. Most protective factors do all three. An important framing: protective factors are not "things you must do, or else". The goal is not to optimise every factor on this list. The goal is to know which ones are strong in your life already (those are your existing sources of strength), which ones are weak or absent (those are your leverage points), and which ones you could realistically strengthen without making well-being itself another stressful obligation.

text: 3.1 Social support and belonging Social support is the most consistently documented protective factor for mental health in the entire research literature — not just in students, but across the lifespan and across cultures. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, the longest-running study of human well-being ever conducted, concluded after more than eighty years that the quality of close relationships in midlife predicted late-life health and happiness more powerfully than any other factor, including income, education, and genetics. The same pattern holds for students: those with at least one or two genuinely close relationships show markedly lower rates of depression and anxiety, and recover faster when they do struggle. Three features of social support matter more than the raw number of contacts. Perceived support — your felt sense that someone would be there for you in a crisis — is more predictive than actual support received. Emotional support (being heard and understood) is more protective than instrumental support (being helped with practical tasks), though both matter. And belonging — the felt sense of being part of a group that values you — is a distinct construct from either, and is particularly important in the student transition years when older belonging structures (family, school, hometown) are loosening and new ones (friend groups, clubs, departments, residence halls) are forming. Belonging is not about popularity. A student with two close friends and one steady community (a club, a sports team, a part-time job, a religious group) often has a stronger sense of belonging than a student with a hundred acquaintances and no steady community. The research on loneliness interventions consistently finds that depth of connection matters more than breadth.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: ne steady community (a club, a sports team, a part-time job, a religious group) often has a stronger sense of belonging than a student with a hundred acquaintances and no steady community. The research on loneliness interventions consistently finds that depth of connection matters more than breadth. Quality over quantity is not a cliché here; it is the empirical finding. A USEFUL SELF-CHECK Name one person you could call at 3 a.m. if you were in trouble. Name one group or community in which you feel known. Name one place on or near campus where you feel you belong. If any of these is hard to answer, Chapter 6 has concrete suggestions for how to build them — and how long it realistically takes. 3.2 Sleep quality Sleep was covered as a risk factor in Chapter 2; here we reframe it as a protective factor, because the relationship runs in both directions. Just as poor sleep raises depression risk, good sleep is one of the strongest protective factors

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: against both depression and anxiety, and is one of the strongest predictors of recovery when symptoms are present. Many students who believe they have treatment-resistant depression or anxiety are, on closer inspection, chronically sleep-deprived; restoring sleep produces substantial improvement without any other intervention. "Good sleep" in the protective sense is not just about total hours, though that matters. It is about consistency (similar bed and wake times across the week, including weekends), timing (sleep that aligns with your circadian rhythm, which for most young adults means sleeping roughly 11 p.m. to 7 a.m.), continuity (few awakenings, and quick return to sleep when they happen), and sufficiency (seven to nine hours for most young adults). The detailed practices for achieving these are in Chapter 4. 3.3 Regular physical movement If sleep is the most biologically direct protective factor, physical movement is the second. Across hundreds of studies and dozens of meta-analyses, regular moderate physical activity is associated with lower rates of depression and anxiety, faster recovery from both, and lower risk of relapse. The effect sizes are not trivial: in some meta-analyses, regular exercise compares favourably with first-line treatments for mild to moderate depression. The mechanisms are multiple — improved sleep, reduced inflammation, increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF, a protein that supports neural growth and resilience), social contact if the activity is done with others, time in nature if the activity is outdoors, and a sense of agency and accomplishment that counters the helplessness central to depression. "Regular physical movement" deserves unpacking.

"Regular physical movement" deserves unpacking. The evidence base points to moderate-intensity aerobic activity (brisk walking, cycling, swimming, dancing) for roughly 150 minutes per week, plus some strength training (bodyweight exercises, weights, climbing, yoga) on two or more days per week, as a target associated with substantial mental-health benefits. But the relationship is dose-dependent from zero — meaning that any movement is better than none, and the largest jump in benefit comes from going from sedentary to even small amounts of regular activity. The student who is currently doing nothing does not need to train for a marathon. Walking twenty minutes a day, four days a week, is a meaningful intervention. It is also worth naming what movement is not a substitute for. Exercise is not a treatment for severe depression, eating-disorder recovery, trauma work, or any condition in which professional support is warranted. The "exercise cures

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: everything" framing is well-meaning but, for students with significant symptoms, can become a guilt-inducing demand. The relationship between movement and mental health is real and substantial; it is also partial. Use it as one protective layer among several. 150 min/week The moderate-intensity movement target most consistently associated with mental-health benefits in students. But any movement is better than none — the curve is steepest at the low end. 3.4 Flourishing, meaning, and purpose Flourishing is a slightly awkward word for an important concept: the experience of functioning well, not just feeling good. The psychologist Corey Keyes, who developed the most widely used measure of flourishing, defined it as a combination of emotional well-being (positive affect, life satisfaction), psychological well-being (self-acceptance, personal growth, purpose, environmental mastery, autonomy, positive relations), and social well-being (social acceptance, social actualisation, social contribution, social coherence, social integration). A student can be flourishing even on days when they feel sad, and a student can have low flourishing even on days when they feel fine — because flourishing is about how your life is going over time, not how you feel in a given moment. Flourishing is protective against depression and anxiety in two ways. First, it represents a higher baseline — the higher your baseline of well-being, the further you have to fall before reaching clinical concern. Second, the components of flourishing (especially purpose, growth, and positive relations) actively counter the psychological processes that drive depression: hopelessness, helplessness, self-criticism, and isolation.

Second, the components of flourishing (especially purpose, growth, and positive relations) actively counter the psychological processes that drive depression: hopelessness, helplessness, self-criticism, and isolation. A student who feels that their life has direction and meaning is more resilient to academic setbacks, relationship breakups, and the inevitable disappointments of early adulthood. Purpose does not require a grand mission. It can be as specific as "I want to become a teacher" or as broad as "I want to be a good friend and leave things better than I found them". What matters is that the purpose feels genuinely yours, that it connects to something larger than your immediate comfort, and that it is actionable in daily life. Many students experience a "purpose gap" in the university years — the old certainties about who they are and what they are for have loosened, and new ones have not yet formed. This is a developmental task, not a deficiency. It takes time, experimentation, and often a few false starts.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: A SMALL REFLECTION What is one thing in the last week that gave you a sense of meaning or being fully yourself? It does not need to be impressive. It might be a conversation, a moment of focus on a piece of work, a small kindness, a creative act, a walk in a place you love. Noticing these moments is itself a flourishing practice. 3.5 Self-compassion Self-compassion, as defined by the researcher Kristin Neff, has three components: self-kindness (treating yourself with the same warmth you would offer a friend) instead of harsh self-judgment; common humanity (recognising that struggle is part of being human, not a personal failing) instead of isolation; and mindful awareness (noting your pain without suppressing it or overidentifying with it) instead of rumination. Self-compassion is not the same as self-esteem, which is contingent on evaluations of worth and tends to collapse precisely when it is most needed. Self-compassion is available regardless of how you are doing. Across many studies, self-compassion is associated with lower rates of depression and anxiety, lower perfectionism, lower fear of failure, greater resilience after setbacks, and healthier relationships. It is also one of the few protective factors that can be cultivated relatively quickly — brief structured practices, often taking ten minutes a day for a few weeks, have been shown in randomised trials to produce measurable improvements in self-compassion and reductions in self-criticism. Chapter 10 includes several such practices. The most common misconception about self-compassion is that it will lower your standards or make you lazy. The evidence is the opposite.

The most common misconception about self-compassion is that it will lower your standards or make you lazy. The evidence is the opposite. Self-compassionate students tend to take more responsibility for failures (because the cost of admitting a mistake is lower when you are not also attacking yourself for it), persist longer at difficult tasks, and recover more quickly from setbacks. Selfcriticism, by contrast, is associated with procrastination, avoidance, and worse performance over time — not because self-critical students do not care, but because the emotional cost of trying is so high. 3.6 Help-seeking attitudes Willingness to seek help when you need it is, paradoxically, one of the strongest protective factors against the worsening of mental-health conditions. Students who hold positive attitudes toward help-seeking — who believe that asking for

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: support is reasonable, that counselling is effective, that mental-health struggles are not shameful — tend to access support earlier, when problems are more manageable, and recover faster. Students who hold negative attitudes tend to delay, sometimes for years, by which point problems have often compounded. Help-seeking attitudes are shaped by many things: cultural background, family messages about vulnerability, prior experiences with helpers (positive or negative), gender norms (men, on average, hold more negative attitudes), and the perceived accessibility and cultural responsiveness of the support available. The attitudes are not fixed. Exposure to stories of peers who have sought help and benefited, conversations with trusted mentors, and even brief contact with a sympathetic counsellor can shift them substantially. It is worth noting that "help-seeking" includes a wide range of behaviours, not only formal counselling. Talking to a friend, a family member, a religious leader, a peer supporter, an academic advisor, or a GP can all be forms of help-seeking. The protective factor is not "going to therapy" specifically; it is the willingness to acknowledge distress and let another person in. Chapter 13 walks through the range of options in detail. 3.7 Routine and structure It is unglamorous but well-established: students with regular daily routines show lower rates of depression and anxiety than students with chaotic schedules, even when total sleep, study time, and social contact are held constant. Routine is protective for several reasons. It reduces the cognitive load of constant decision-making. It anchors sleep and meal timing, which in turn anchors circadian rhythm.

It reduces the cognitive load of constant decision-making. It anchors sleep and meal timing, which in turn anchors circadian rhythm. It provides a sense of agency and predictability that buffers against the unpredictability of student life. And it makes healthy behaviours the default rather than something that requires willpower every time. "Routine" does not mean rigidity. A good routine has anchors — fixed points around which the day is organised (a regular wake time, a regular meal time, a regular study block) — and flexibility in between. It is also personal: a routine that works for a morning person will not work for an evening person, and a routine that works during term will not work during exam week or holidays. The goal is not to find the perfect schedule but to have some schedule, and to revisit it when it stops serving you.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 3.8 Connection to nature Time in natural environments — parks, forests, coastlines, even well-treed urban streets — is associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, and perceived stress, and with improved attention and mood. The mechanisms are likely multiple: exposure to natural light (which supports circadian rhythm and vitamin D synthesis), reduced exposure to the sensory overload of urban environments, the invitation to slower breathing and walking pace, and the cognitive restoration that comes from what environmental psychologists call "soft fascination" — the gentle, effortless attention that natural scenes invite. For students, the practical implication is not that you need to retreat to a forest. It is that some regular contact with nature — a walk through a park on the way to class, studying outside on good-weather days, a weekend hike, even tending a small plant in your room — appears to confer measurable benefit. The effect has been documented with as little as 120 minutes per week in natural settings, and the benefit flattens out beyond that — meaning you do not need to live in a national park to get most of the upside. 3.9 Cognitive flexibility Cognitive flexibility is the capacity to shift perspectives, consider alternative interpretations of events, and adjust your behaviour when circumstances change. It is the opposite of rumination (the repetitive, narrowly focused negative thinking central to depression) and of rigid all-or-nothing thinking (central to anxiety and perfectionism). It is also one of the few protective factors that can be deliberately strengthened through practice. Cognitive flexibility is not the same as positive thinking, which can shade into denial. It is the ability to hold multiple honest interpretations of an event at once.

Cognitive flexibility is not the same as positive thinking, which can shade into denial. It is the ability to hold multiple honest interpretations of an event at once. A flexible response to a poor grade, for example, might be: "This grade is disappointing, and it does not define my ability or my future, and I can learn from what went wrong, and I am allowed to feel upset about it for a while." An inflexible response might be: "I am bad at this subject, I will never succeed, this proves I should drop out." Same event, very different consequences for mood and behaviour. The practices in Chapter 10 — mindfulness, self-compassion, journaling, perspective-taking — are largely cognitive flexibility practices. They work not by changing what happens to you but by widening the space between event and interpretation, in which your own agency lives.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 3.10 Financial stability and basic-needs security Just as financial stress is a powerful risk factor, financial stability and basicneeds security are powerful protective factors. The student who knows their rent, food, and tuition are covered has substantially more cognitive and emotional bandwidth for everything else — academic work, social connection, sleep, exercise, identity exploration — than the student who is constantly calculating trade-offs. This is not a personal virtue; it is a structural condition. The protective factor here is not "being responsible with money" but actually having enough, which is shaped far more by family wealth, financial aid policy, national student support systems, and labour market conditions than by individual choices. For students who do not have the protective factor of financial stability, the equivalent protective move is knowing how to access the support that does exist: emergency aid funds, food pantries, government benefits, fee waivers, scholarships, and basic-needs navigation services on campus. Chapter 8 walks through these in detail. Knowing the landscape does not erase the underlying stress, but it reduces the additional cognitive load of not knowing where to turn when a crisis hits. 3.11 Spiritual, religious, or philosophical practice For students who hold a spiritual, religious, or philosophical practice, that practice can be a substantial protective factor.

The mechanisms are several: a framework for meaning-making in the face of suffering, a community of shared practice, regular rituals that structure time and provide emotional regulation, practices of prayer or meditation that overlap with evidence-based contemplative techniques, and an ethical orientation that can counter some of the individualism and achievement-orientation of university life. It is worth noting that the protective effect is not uniform across all forms of religious or spiritual involvement. Forms that emphasise a benevolent relationship with the divine and a supportive community are generally protective; forms that emphasise divine punishment, exclusivity, or conflict with one's identity (particularly around sexuality or gender) can be risk factors in their own right. The protective factor is not "religion" in the abstract but a specific kind of relationship with meaning, community, and the transcendent.

That response, while understandable, is the opposite of what protective factors are for. A more useful exercise is to read the list as an inventory of your current strengths and your current leverage points. title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: The remaining chapters in this guide go into depth on the protective factors most amenable to change: sleep (Chapter 4), movement (Chapter 5), social connection (Chapter 6), academic habits (Chapter 7), financial wellness (Chapter 8), digital boundaries (Chapter 9), mindfulness and self-compassion (Chapter 10), and identity and belonging (Chapter 12). They are not a checklist. They are a menu. Pick what speaks to your current life, and trust that strengthening one protective factor tends, over time, to strengthen several. CHAPTER 4 Sleep and Circadian Health If there is a single habit most worth protecting in student life, it is sleep. Almost every other protective factor in this guide is harder to maintain when sleep is short, and easier when sleep is sufficient. SAFETY NOTE This chapter covers sleep hygiene and circadian health for general well-being. It does not address diagnosed sleep disorders. If you suspect you have sleep apnoea, narcolepsy, restless legs syndrome, or another sleep disorder, please consult a physician — these conditions require clinical assessment, not lifestyle changes. Sleep is the foundation on which almost every other mental-health-relevant process rests. During sleep, the brain consolidates the day's learning into longterm memory, processes emotional experiences, clears metabolic waste products (including amyloid-beta, the protein implicated in Alzheimer's disease), regulates the hormones that control appetite and stress, and recalibrates the neural circuits that govern mood and attention. None of this is optional. None of it can be done while awake. And almost all of it is degraded when sleep is short, fragmented, or mistimed. The student-specific challenge is that university life is structurally hostile to good sleep.

And almost all of it is degraded when sleep is short, fragmented, or mistimed. The student-specific challenge is that university life is structurally hostile to good sleep. Late classes, social events that run into the early hours, shared living spaces with mismatched schedules, the ease of streaming another episode, the constant cognitive activation of unfinished academic work, the social pressure to be available late at night, and the widespread use of caffeine and alcohol all conspire to push bedtimes later and fragment the sleep that does occur. Add the biologically driven circadian shift of late adolescence — which pushes the natural bedtime of an eighteen-year-old roughly two hours later than that of a forty-year-old — and you have a perfect recipe for chronic sleep deprivation disguised as normal student life.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 4.1 How much sleep do students actually need? The National Sleep Foundation and most major health bodies recommend seven to nine hours of sleep per night for young adults (eighteen to twenty-five). Most students need somewhere in this range, with individual variation. A useful way to find your own number: on a week when you have no alarm, no deadlines, and no social pressure to be up at a particular time, how many hours do you sleep before waking naturally? That number, give or take thirty minutes, is your sleep need. For most students it falls between seven and a half and nine hours. The gap between need and reality is striking. In the Healthy Minds Study and similar surveys, the median student reports sleeping six hours or less on weekdays — a deficit of ninety minutes to three hours per night compared to their need. Over a week, that compounds into ten to twenty hours of sleep debt, which the brain does not simply "make up" by sleeping in on Saturday. The cognitive and emotional effects of chronic partial sleep deprivation — even at modest deficits — are well documented: reduced attention, poorer memory consolidation, slower reaction time, impaired judgment, greater emotional reactivity, lower frustration tolerance, and, over months, measurably higher rates of depression and anxiety. 7–9 hrs The recommended nightly sleep range for young adults. The median student reports six hours or less — a chronic deficit with measurable effects on mood, attention, and resilience. 4.2 The two things that matter most: when you wake, and when you see light If you remember only two things from this chapter, remember these. First, your wake time sets your biological clock more powerfully than your bedtime does.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: c deficit with measurable effects on mood, attention, and resilience. 4.2 The two things that matter most: when you wake, and when you see light If you remember only two things from this chapter, remember these. First, your wake time sets your biological clock more powerfully than your bedtime does. The brain's master clock (the suprachiasmatic nucleus, in the hypothalamus) takes its primary cue from the onset of light in the morning. Waking at a consistent time, seven days a week, anchors your circadian rhythm and makes falling asleep at a reasonable hour the following night far easier. Sleeping in on weekends — the classic student pattern — produces what chronobiologists call "social jetlag": the body clock drifts later by two or three hours over the weekend, then is jolted back early on Monday morning, producing the cognitive and emotional equivalent of flying across several time zones every week.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Second, morning light exposure is the single most powerful external signal your brain uses to set its clock. Getting bright light into your eyes within thirty to sixty minutes of waking — ideally outside, even on an overcast day (outdoor light is far brighter than indoor light, even when it does not feel that way) — produces a cascade of effects: it suppresses lingering melatonin (the sleepiness hormone), raises cortisol to its appropriate morning peak, advances your circadian rhythm so that you become sleepy earlier in the evening, and improves mood directly through pathways that are not fully understood but are well documented. Fifteen to thirty minutes of outdoor light in the first hour of waking is one of the highest-leverage sleep interventions available, and it is free. THE TWO ANCHORS 1. Wake at the same time every day, including weekends, within a thirtyminute window. 2. Get bright outdoor light into your eyes within an hour of waking, for at least fifteen minutes. If you do nothing else from this chapter, do these two. They will, over a few weeks, move your bedtime earlier and improve your sleep quality without any direct effort on bedtime itself. 4.3 The evening wind-down The two anchors above handle the morning. The evening requires a different set of practices, all aimed at one goal: allowing your nervous system to shift from the sympathetic activation of the day into the parasympathetic state required for sleep. You cannot make yourself sleep, any more than you can make yourself fall in love. You can only create the conditions in which sleep becomes possible, and then let it arrive. LIGHT MANAGEMENT Just as morning light advances your clock and signals daytime, evening light delays your clock and signals daytime-extended.

LIGHT MANAGEMENT Just as morning light advances your clock and signals daytime, evening light delays your clock and signals daytime-extended. The brain is particularly sensitive to blue-spectrum light (the kind emitted by screens, LED bulbs, and many overhead lights), which directly suppresses melatonin production. The ideal evening light environment is dim, warm-toned, and indirect — think lamplight rather than overhead fluorescents, and warm amber rather than cool white. Practically: in the two hours before bed, lower the lights in your room, switch devices to night-shift or warm-colour modes, and consider using a small warmtoned reading lamp rather than a full-spectrum screen.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: SCREEN USE IN BED The single most common sleep-disruptive habit in students is the use of phones, tablets, or laptops in bed. The disruption is twofold: the light suppresses melatonin (as above), and the content — whether social media, news, video, or messaging — produces cognitive and emotional activation that is the opposite of the wind-down state. Even apparently "relaxing" content (a film, a feed of funny videos) keeps the brain in a state of vigilance that delays sleep onset and fragments the sleep that follows. The most protective practice is also the simplest: keep screens out of the bed entirely. Charge your phone across the room, not on the nightstand. Use a physical alarm clock if you need one. Treat the bed as a place for sleep (and intimacy), not for content consumption. This is hard. The phone-in-bed pattern is reinforced by social norms, by the fear of missing messages, by the use of the phone as an alarm, and — for many students — by the use of the phone as the last social contact of the day. The shift is worth making anyway. Most students who manage it report, within two to three weeks, that they fall asleep faster, wake less in the night, and feel more rested in the morning. The first week is difficult; the habit stabilises quickly after that. CAFFEINE Caffeine is the most widely used psychoactive substance in the world, and the most common pharmacological disruptor of student sleep. Its half-life — the time it takes for the body to eliminate half of a given dose — is approximately five to six hours in healthy adults, but varies considerably (up to ten hours in some people). This means that a coffee consumed at 4 p.m. still has half its caffeine active in your system at 9 to 10 p.m., and a quarter of it active at 2 to 4 a.m.

text: to eliminate half of a given dose — is approximately five to six hours in healthy adults, but varies considerably (up to ten hours in some people). This means that a coffee consumed at 4 p.m. still has half its caffeine active in your system at 9 to 10 p.m., and a quarter of it active at 2 to 4 a.m. Caffeine blocks adenosine, the neurotransmitter that builds up during wakefulness and produces sleep pressure; with adenosine blocked, you do not feel sleepy even when your brain needs sleep. The practical guidance, supported by sleep research, is to stop consuming caffeine by early afternoon — ideally 2 p.m., and no later than 4 p.m. for most people. This includes coffee, most teas, energy drinks, many soft drinks, and some pain medications. Decaf coffee is not caffeine-free; a typical cup contains 2 to 15 mg of caffeine (compared to 80 to 200 mg in regular coffee), which is usually fine in the evening but worth knowing. If you are caffeine-sensitive or a slow metaboliser, an earlier cutoff will help.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: ALCOHOL Alcohol is often misperceived as a sleep aid because it produces sedation. It is, in fact, a major disruptor of sleep quality. While it may shorten the time to fall asleep, it suppresses REM sleep in the first half of the night (the stage most involved in emotional processing and memory consolidation), causes fragmentation and awakening in the second half as it is metabolised, worsens snoring and sleep apnoea, and produces a net loss of restorative sleep even when total time in bed is normal. The cumulative effect of regular evening drinking on student mood and cognition is substantial and often underestimated. The practical guidance: if you choose to drink, do so earlier in the evening rather than right before bed, keep quantities moderate, and recognise that even one or two drinks will measurably reduce the restorative quality of that night's sleep. The "I sleep fine after a drink" perception is usually a misread of sedation as sleep. COGNITIVE OFFLOADING Many students struggle to fall asleep because their minds begin processing the day's events and tomorrow's tasks the moment they lie down. This is not a character flaw; it is what the brain does when it has not had a dedicated time and space for that processing. A simple, evidence-based practice is the "brain dump": ten or fifteen minutes before bed, write down everything on your mind — tasks for tomorrow, unfinished conversations, worries, ideas. The act of externalising them reduces the cognitive load of holding them in working memory and signals to the brain that they are safely stored elsewhere. Many students who try this report a noticeable reduction in sleep-onset latency within a week.

Many students who try this report a noticeable reduction in sleep-onset latency within a week. 4.4 What to do if you cannot sleep Even with perfect sleep hygiene, there will be nights when you cannot sleep — because of stress, because of a late coffee, because of a disrupted routine, or for no obvious reason at all. How you respond to a bad night matters more than the bad night itself. The most common mistake is to stay in bed, increasingly anxious about not sleeping, calculating the hours until the alarm, and inadvertently conditioning the brain to associate the bed with wakefulness and anxiety. This is how acute insomnia becomes chronic.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: THE 20-MINUTE RULE If you have been in bed for roughly twenty minutes and are not asleep — and especially if you are feeling frustrated — get up. Go to another room, keep the lights low, and do something calm and not screen-based: read a physical book, stretch, listen to a quiet podcast, do a brief breathing exercise. Return to bed only when you feel genuinely sleepy. Repeat as many times as needed. This protects the bed-sleep association and prevents the spiral of sleep anxiety. The day after a bad night, two things help. First, do not "catch up" by sleeping in or napping extensively. A short nap (twenty to thirty minutes, before 3 p.m.) is fine; a three-hour afternoon nap or sleeping until noon will shift your body clock and perpetuate the problem. Second, get bright light and some movement early in the day, and resist the temptation to over-caffeinate. The goal is to build sleep pressure through the day so that the following night's sleep comes easily and resets the cycle. 4.5 Naps: use carefully Naps can be a useful tool for managing sleep debt, but they are easy to misuse. The evidence base points to a few principles. Short is better than long — naps of ten to twenty minutes produce alertness and mood benefits without significant sleep inertia (the grogginess that comes from waking from deep sleep). Naps longer than thirty minutes enter deep sleep and produce more inertia than benefit, unless you complete a full ninety-minute cycle. Early is better than late — napping before 3 p.m. is unlikely to disrupt that night's sleep; napping after 4 p.m. often will. Consistency helps — if you nap regularly at the same time, your body learns to expect it and the nap becomes more restorative. Naps are not a substitute for insufficient nighttime sleep.

Consistency helps — if you nap regularly at the same time, your body learns to expect it and the nap becomes more restorative. Naps are not a substitute for insufficient nighttime sleep. A student who is sleeping five hours a night and "catching up" with daily naps is still chronically sleep-deprived, even if the naps take the edge off. Use naps as a supplement to adequate nighttime sleep, not as a replacement for it. 4.6 Chronotype: working with, not against, your biology Chronotype is the natural tendency of your body to sleep at a particular time — popularised as "morning larks" versus "night owls", though the reality is a continuum. Chronotype is partly genetic, partly age-dependent (late adolescence and early adulthood skew later; midlife and beyond skew earlier), and not a moral failing. The student who genuinely cannot fall asleep before 1

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: a.m. and genuinely cannot wake before 9 a.m. is not lazy or undisciplined; they are operating on a different biological schedule than the student who naturally wakes at 6 a.m. The challenge is that much of university life — early lectures, exams scheduled for 9 a.m., institutional expectations of morning productivity — is built around morning-type schedules, which disadvantages evening-type students. Where you have flexibility, work with your chronotype: schedule demanding cognitive work for your personal peak hours (which, for evening types, may be late afternoon or evening), protect your morning sleep if your schedule allows, and advocate for yourself with advisors and disability services if early starts are producing genuine dysfunction. That said, chronotype is not infinitely malleable but is also not fixed. The two anchors above — consistent wake time and morning light — can shift an evening chronotype earlier by an hour or two over several weeks, which can make a meaningful practical difference. The goal is not to force yourself into a schedule that fights your biology, but to find the latest schedule that still allows you to function in the institutional structures you need to navigate.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: These signs do not mean something is fundamentally wrong with you. They mean a clinician should help you figure out what is going on. Sleep disorders are common, frequently missed in student populations, and often highly treatable. The fastest route to better sleep, in those cases, is professional assessment, not more sleep-hygiene tips. "You cannot always control when you sleep. You can almost always control when you wake, and when you see light. Start there." Chapter 5 turns to the body in motion — the second major biological protective factor, and the one most tightly linked to sleep in its effects on mood. CHAPTER 5 Movement, Body, and Mood The body and the mind are not separate systems that happen to share an address. They are one system, and what you do with your body shapes what you feel in your mind. SAFETY NOTE This chapter is about general well-being through movement, nutrition, and substance awareness. It does not provide exercise prescriptions for medical conditions, eating-disorder recovery guidance, or substance-use treatment. If you have a history of disordered eating, please approach the nutrition section with care, and consider reading it with a trusted support person or clinician. The relationship between body and mood is bidirectional, constant, and largely underestimated. When you are depressed, your body slows — movements become effortful, posture collapses, breathing shallows, facial expression flattens. When your body is held in a slow, collapsed, shallow state for long periods — sitting at a desk for hours, scrolling on a phone, lying in bed — your mood tends to follow. The brain is constantly reading the body's signals and inferring an emotional state from them. If the body says "I am exhausted and shut down", the brain is inclined to agree.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: This is not a claim that you can posture or stretch your way out of depression. It is a claim that the body is one of the levers through which mood is regulated, and that small changes in how you hold and move your body can produce meaningful shifts in how you feel. The lever is not magic, but it is real, and it is one of the most accessible protective factors available to a student. 5.1 What kind of movement, and how much? The research literature on exercise and mental health is large and occasionally contradictory, but a few consistent findings emerge. Moderate-intensity aerobic activity — brisk walking, jogging, cycling, swimming, dancing, rowing, anything that raises your heart rate to roughly 60 to 75 percent of maximum and sustains it — produces the largest and most reliable mood benefits. Resistance training (weightlifting, bodyweight exercises, resistance bands) shows comparable benefits for depression and may be particularly helpful for anxiety. Mind-body practices like yoga, tai chi, and qigong show robust benefits for anxiety in particular, likely through their combination of movement, breath regulation, and meditative attention. High-intensity interval training shows benefits but is harder to sustain and carries higher injury risk for sedentary beginners. The most-studied dose is roughly 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity activity, plus two sessions of resistance training. This is the same target recommended for general cardiovascular health, and it is associated in metaanalyses with a roughly 25 to 30 percent reduction in depression risk. But — and this is important — the dose-response curve is steepest at the low end.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 5.2 Practical movement for student lives University life does not always make movement easy. Gym memberships may be expensive or intimidating; schedules may be irregular; weather may be uncooperative; shared living spaces may be small. The good news is that almost none of the mental-health benefit of movement requires a gym, special equipment, or large blocks of time. What follows is a menu of realistic options, not a prescription. Walking The single most accessible form of movement. Twenty to thirty minutes a day, ideally outside. Walking to campus instead of taking the bus, taking the stairs, walking between buildings for breaks, walking with a friend (which doubles as social connection). Active transport Cycling to campus, skateboarding, using a scooter. Combines transportation and exercise, which is one of the most reliable ways to maintain a movement habit without finding additional time. Bodyweight exercise Push-ups, squats, lunges, planks, yoga flows. Requires no equipment, can be done in a small room, and provides both strength and mobility benefits. Many free, high-quality routines are available online (Yoga with Adriene, the NHS fitness studio, etc.). Group classes Many universities offer free or low-cost group fitness classes. The scheduled structure and social element can help students who struggle to maintain a solo habit. Dance, martial arts, climbing, and team sports all count.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Running / jogging Time-efficient and moodelevating, especially outdoors. Couch-to-5k programmes are a well-designed gradual entry point for beginners. Run with a friend or club for accountability. Swimming Particularly good for students with joint issues, asthma, or high anxiety. The water provides sensory regulation that some students find uniquely calming. Often available cheaply through university pools. 5.3 The mood-while-moving effect One of the most reliable findings in exercise psychology is that a single bout of moderate exercise produces an immediate, short-term improvement in mood — reduced anxiety, increased positive affect, improved cognitive function — that lasts for one to three hours afterward. This "acute" effect is distinct from the longer-term benefits of regular exercise and is one of the most practically useful tools in the student mental-health toolkit. A twenty-minute walk before a stressful seminar, a quick bodyweight routine before an exam, a swim after a difficult conversation — these are not workouts in the fitness sense; they are mood regulation in real time. The implication is that movement can be deployed strategically, not just habitually. If you know a particular class or meeting reliably raises your anxiety, scheduling fifteen minutes of movement beforehand is one of the most effective interventions available. If you find yourself ruminating in the evening, a walk outside often breaks the loop more effectively than another hour of trying to think your way out of it. Movement is not just "good for you in general"; it is a tool you can use for specific situations, in real time.

Movement is not just "good for you in general"; it is a tool you can use for specific situations, in real time. 5.4 Outdoor time, light, and nature Movement done outdoors is, on average, more beneficial for mood than the same movement done indoors — likely because of the combined effects of natural light (which supports circadian regulation and vitamin D synthesis), the cognitive restoration of natural environments (the "soft fascination" mentioned in Chapter 3), and the simple fact that outdoor movement tends to be sustained longer and feels less effortful. The mental-health benefits of "green exercise" — activity in natural settings — are documented across many studies, with effects appearing even in urban parks and quite small green spaces.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: The practical takeaway: when you have a choice, take your movement outside. Walk through a park rather than on a treadmill. Cycle along a river rather than on a stationary bike. Study outside on a blanket rather than at a desk by a window. The combined protective effects of movement, light, and nature are larger than any of the three alone. 5.5 Nutrition: basics, not diet culture Nutrition occupies an awkward place in student mental-health guides. On one hand, what you eat genuinely affects how you feel — through blood sugar regulation, gut-brain signalling, nutrient status, and the simple fact that hungry or undernourished students struggle to regulate mood. On the other hand, the cultural space around food and body is saturated with misinformation, moralism, and disordered eating patterns, and a well-meaning chapter on nutrition can easily become a trigger for students with eating disorders or body-image struggles. What follows is deliberately basic, deliberately non-prescriptive, and deliberately framed around adequacy rather than restriction. The goal is not to optimise your diet; it is to make sure that food is supporting your mood rather than undermining it. EAT ENOUGH The most common nutrition-related cause of low mood and anxiety in students is simply not eating enough — either because of food insecurity (see Chapter 8), because of skipped meals due to a chaotic schedule, or because of restrictive eating patterns. The brain runs on glucose; when blood sugar drops, mood drops, attention drops, irritability rises, and anxiety increases. Eating regular meals — three meals a day, plus snacks as needed — is more protective of mood than the specific composition of those meals.

Eating regular meals — three meals a day, plus snacks as needed — is more protective of mood than the specific composition of those meals. If you are skipping breakfast and lunch and eating one large meal in the evening, your mood and concentration are paying for it. EAT REASONABLY A "reasonable" diet, in the evidence-based sense, looks roughly like: plenty of vegetables and fruit (whatever is affordable and accessible); adequate protein (beans, lentils, eggs, dairy, fish, meat, tofu — whatever fits your preferences and budget); some whole grains; some healthy fats (olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, oily fish); and limited but not zero intake of highly processed foods, sugary drinks, and alcohol. The Mediterranean diet pattern has the strongest evidence

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: base for mental health, but the specific pattern matters less than the basics: enough food, regular meals, some plants, some protein, not too much sugar or alcohol. CAFFEINE Caffeine was covered in Chapter 4 in the context of sleep. From a mood perspective, low to moderate caffeine intake (up to roughly 400 mg per day — about four cups of coffee) is associated with improved alertness, concentration, and mood for most people. Higher intake, and intake later in the day, produces anxiety, jitteriness, and disrupted sleep — which then worsens mood the next day. If you notice your anxiety rising with your caffeine intake, the relationship is probably causal, not coincidental. ALCOHOL Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. While it produces short-term relaxation and disinhibition, it worsens mood over the following one to three days, disrupts sleep (see Chapter 4), interacts dangerously with many medications, and is associated with substantially higher rates of depression and anxiety in students who drink heavily. Low-risk drinking guidelines (when not contraindicated by medication, pregnancy, or personal history) suggest no more than fourteen drinks per week for men and women, with no more than four drinks on any single occasion for women and five for men. Many students exceed these guidelines without recognising it, particularly in cultures where heavy weekend drinking is normative. OTHER SUBSTANCES Cannabis, nicotine, prescription stimulants used non-medically, and other recreational substances all have documented relationships with student mental health, covered briefly in Chapter 2.

The general principle: any substance that produces short-term relief or enhancement at the cost of sleep, mood, or functioning in the following days is, on balance, working against you. The occasional use may be fine; the regular use-as-coping is a warning sign. If you are using substances to manage distress, please talk to a counsellor or doctor — not because you are in trouble, but because there are usually more effective and less costly ways to address the underlying distress. 5.6 Movement and eating-disorder recovery For students in recovery from an eating disorder, or with a complicated relationship with food and exercise, much of the standard advice in this chapter needs modification. Movement that becomes compulsive, food rules that

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: become restrictive, and body-tracking that becomes obsessive can all masquerade as "healthy habits" while actively undermining recovery. If this resonates with you, please consider working with a clinician who specialises in eating disorders — the principles of recovery are specific, evidence-based, and very difficult to navigate alone. University counselling services and student health services can refer you to appropriate specialists. 5.7 A note on body image Body image is a significant mental-health issue in its own right for many students, and one that intersects with movement, food, and mood in complex ways. The cultural pressure to achieve a particular body shape — intensified by social media, fitness marketing, and peer comparison — can turn the protective practices of movement and eating into sources of distress. A student who exercises primarily to alter their body, and who feels anxious or self-punishing when they cannot, is not getting the mental-health benefits of movement; they are getting a different problem dressed up as self-care. The reframe worth considering: movement is for what your body can do, not for how it looks. Strength, endurance, flexibility, balance, the capacity to walk up a hill without breathlessness, the capacity to play with a child, the capacity to recover from an injury — these are the meaningful outcomes of movement, and they are achievable at almost any body shape and size. If your movement practice is making you more preoccupied with your body, it is worth asking whether the practice is serving you or serving a cultural script you did not choose. "Move because it changes how you feel, not because it changes how you look. The first is reliably achievable.

The second is a trap." 5.8 Building a sustainable movement habit Most students do not have a movement problem; they have a habit-formation problem. The following principles, drawn from the behaviour-change literature, make habit formation substantially easier. Start absurdly small. A daily five-minute walk is a better foundation than a three-times-weekly hour at the gym, because the daily practice is more likely to stick. You can scale up later; first establish the habit.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Attach to an existing anchor. "I will walk for ten minutes after my morning class" is more likely to stick than "I will walk more". The anchor makes the cue automatic. Reduce friction. Lay out your workout clothes the night before. Keep walking shoes by the door. Choose a movement you can do without travelling far. Friction is the enemy of consistency. Make it social. Walking with a friend, joining a class, signing up for a club sport — social commitment converts movement from a willpower task to a relational one, which is far more durable. Track without obsessing. A simple checkmark on a calendar is enough. Detailed tracking apps can help but can also become a source of pressure and perfectionism. Expect lapses and plan for them. A missed day is not a failed habit; it is a normal part of the process. The students who maintain movement long-term are not the ones who never miss; they are the ones who return to it after missing. Choose activities you actually like. The "best" form of movement is the one you will do. If you hate running, do not run. Walk, dance, swim, climb, cycle, garden. Movement you enjoy is movement you will repeat. Chapter 6 moves from the body to one of the most important protective factors of all: social connection and the experience of belonging. CHAPTER 6 Social Connection and Belonging We are social primates wired for connection. The single most powerful protective factor for student mental health is the quality of your close relationships — and the most powerful risk factor is their absence. SAFETY NOTE This chapter addresses loneliness and social difficulty in general terms. It does not address abusive relationships, harassment, or assault.
