title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: The previous chapter explained how movement protects the brain. This chapter explains how other people do. The evidence is overwhelming: across decades of research, across cultures, across the lifespan, the quality of close relationships is the single strongest predictor of human well-being. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, following hundreds of men (and eventually their partners and children) for more than eighty years, found that the quality of relationships in midlife predicted health and happiness in late life more powerfully than income, education, social class, IQ, or genetics. The finding has been replicated in many other cohorts. The shape of the relationship is consistent: closeness matters; isolation harms; the effect is large. For students, this finding lands at a particularly delicate moment. The transition to university loosens the older belonging structures — family, school, hometown, childhood friendships — before the new ones have fully formed. The first weeks and months of university are often experienced as profoundly lonely, even by students who appear socially successful from the outside. And the modern student environment, with its heavy use of digital communication, its competitive academic culture, and its often fragmented social geography, can make the formation of deep connection harder than at any previous point in the student's life. 6.1 Alone versus lonely: a critical distinction Solitude and loneliness are not the same thing, and confusing them causes a great deal of unnecessary suffering. Solitude is the physical state of being alone. It can be restorative, creative, deeply enjoyable — many people, including many students, need regular solitude to function well.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: istinction Solitude and loneliness are not the same thing, and confusing them causes a great deal of unnecessary suffering. Solitude is the physical state of being alone. It can be restorative, creative, deeply enjoyable — many people, including many students, need regular solitude to function well. Loneliness is the subjective distress that arises from the gap between the social connection you want and the social connection you have. You can feel lonely in a crowd, lonely in a relationship, lonely at a party. You can also be alone for an entire weekend and feel perfectly content. The practical importance of this distinction is that the antidote to loneliness is not always more people. Sometimes it is — when you are genuinely isolated, more contact is the answer. But often the antidote is deeper connection with the people already in your life, or a shift in the quality of your relationship with yourself when you are alone. The student who has a hundred acquaintances and no one to call at 3 a.m. is lonely in a way that no quantity of additional acquaintances will fix. The student with two close friends and a rich inner life when alone is not lonely at all.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: A USEFUL SELF-CHECK In the last week, how many conversations did you have that felt genuinely connecting — where you felt seen and where you saw the other person? One or two such conversations per week is associated with substantially lower loneliness than daily surface-level interactions. 6.2 Why university is uniquely lonely The loneliness of the early university years is not a personal failing. It is a structural feature of the transition. Several specific factors converge: Loss of established community. Family, school friends, teachers, coaches, neighbours — the web of relationships that provided automatic belonging for eighteen years is suddenly loosened. Even if those relationships continue, they are no longer daily and ambient. New social environment without scripts. University social life lacks the structured, repeated contact that school provided. There is no single classroom where everyone sees everyone else daily. Friendships have to be actively built, often from scratch, in environments designed for transience (large lectures, shared residences, short-term group projects). Comparison culture. Students see curated versions of each other's lives on social media and conclude that everyone else is having the time of their life. This makes loneliness feel like a personal failure rather than a near-universal experience of the transition. Identity transition. The self you were in your hometown may not fit naturally in your new environment. Finding people who see and value the new self you are becoming takes time. Practical barriers. Money, transport, scheduling, and the awkwardness of initiating social contact with strangers all make the mechanics of building connection harder than they look.

Money, transport, scheduling, and the awkwardness of initiating social contact with strangers all make the mechanics of building connection harder than they look. The result is that loneliness in the first term of university is closer to the norm than the exception. The Healthy Minds Study finds that more than half of students report moderate to severe loneliness, with peaks in the first year and during examination periods. The loneliness typically eases over the course of the first year as friendships solidify, but for some students it persists and becomes a major contributor to depression and anxiety.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 6.3 How connection is actually built The research on how adults form friendships is surprisingly consistent, and the principles apply directly to students. Repeated, unplanned interaction is the single most important factor. We form friendships with people we see regularly, in contexts where interaction is natural and low-stakes. The classic university examples are residence halls, part-time jobs, recurring student clubs, lab groups, sports teams, and seminar classes. The student who is lonely should look first at where they have repeated, unplanned interaction in their week — and if the answer is "nowhere", that is the leverage point. Shared activity is the second factor. Friendships formed around a shared activity — a sport, a creative project, a cause, an academic interest — form faster and more robustly than friendships formed through conversation alone. The activity provides a script, a purpose, and a reason to meet again. The student who joins one club and attends consistently for a term will, almost without trying, end up with a social network in a way that the student who "tries to make friends" in lectures will not. Vulnerability is the third factor, and the one most students find hardest. Surfacelevel conversation — classes, weather, sports results — can be sustained indefinitely without producing closeness. Closeness requires the gradual exchange of more personal material: worries, hopes, family stories, embarrassing moments, opinions that might not be shared. The exchange does not need to be dramatic; it needs to be slightly more honest than the social norm. A small disclosure from you invites a small disclosure from the other person, and over weeks and months the relationship deepens.

A small disclosure from you invites a small disclosure from the other person, and over weeks and months the relationship deepens. Students who never disclose — out of shyness, fear of judgment, or perfectionism — often find their friendships stuck at the pleasant-but-shallow level indefinitely. THE THREE CONDITIONS FOR FRIENDSHIP 1. Repeated, unplanned interaction (a context where you see the same people regularly without having to engineer it) 2. Shared activity that gives the interaction a purpose 3. Gradual vulnerability that moves the conversation below the surface If your current social life is missing one of these, that is your leverage point. The most common missing factor in lonely students is the first — they have no context of repeated, unplanned interaction. Joining one recurring activity fixes this within weeks.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 6.4 The first-year social myth There is a widespread belief among students that "freshman year friendships are forever" and that if you have not found your people by the end of the first term, you have missed your chance. This is false, but it is corrosive. It creates a selffulfilling prophecy in which students who have not yet found close friends conclude that something is wrong with them, withdraw, and thereby reduce the very social contact that would solve the problem. The actual pattern is much more gradual. Most students make their first round of friends in the first few weeks — often based on proximity (roommates, hallmates, orientation groups) rather than fit. These friendships often thin out over the first year as students discover who they actually click with. Deeper, more durable friendships often form in the second and third years, around shared majors, clubs, off-campus housing, and post-partying life. The student who feels at the end of first year that they have not yet found "their people" is, in most cases, perfectly on schedule. The useful reframe: your social life at university is a multi-year project, not a one-week orientation event. Keep showing up to contexts where you might meet your people. Keep being slightly more honest than is comfortable. Keep being patient with the gap between when you arrive and when you feel you belong. 6.5 Maintaining friendships over distance For many students, the relationships that matter most are the ones they left behind — family, childhood friends, partners. Maintaining these relationships over distance takes deliberate effort, because the ambient contact that sustained them is gone. The following practices are not glamorous but they work: Schedule recurring contact.

text: s that matter most are the ones they left behind — family, childhood friends, partners. Maintaining these relationships over distance takes deliberate effort, because the ambient contact that sustained them is gone. The following practices are not glamorous but they work: Schedule recurring contact. A weekly Sunday phone call with a parent, a fortnightly video call with a school friend, a daily good-morning text to a partner. Recurrence is more important than duration; ten minutes weekly beats two hours monthly. Use voice and video, not just text. Text communication loses tone, facial expression, and the rhythm of conversation. Voice notes are a useful middle ground — more personal than text, less synchronous than a call. Share small daily details, not just major news. Closeness is built from the texture of daily life, not only from the headlines. A photo of your lunch, a complaint about a professor, a small win — these are the material of intimacy.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Be honest about how you are doing. The temptation to perform "everything is great" for people back home is strong, and it cuts them off from the parts of your life that most need their support. Honest updates — including the hard parts — sustain closeness across distance. Visit when you can. In-person contact, even occasional, recharges the relationship in ways that digital contact cannot. Prioritise visits where possible. Let some friendships change shape. Not every friendship from before university will survive the transition, and that is okay. Some friendships become occasional-catch-up relationships rather than daily-contact relationships, and that is a legitimate form of friendship, not a failure. 6.6 Roommate and housemate relationships For residential students, the roommate or housemate relationship is one of the most consequential relationships of the university years — for better or worse. A good roommate can be a primary source of support, structure, and belonging. A difficult one can be a chronic source of stress that disrupts sleep, study, and mood. Most roommate relationships are somewhere in between, and almost all benefit from explicit communication about expectations. The most common sources of roommate conflict are: cleanliness standards, sleep schedules, noise, guests (especially romantic partners), shared belongings, and food. The most effective prevention is an explicit conversation, early in the arrangement, about expectations in each of these areas. Many residence-life programmes provide conversation guides for this. The conversation may feel awkward at the time, but it is far less awkward than months of unspoken resentment. When conflict does arise, the most effective response is direct, specific, and non-accusatory communication.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: WHEN A ROOMMATE SITUATION IS HARMING YOUR MENTAL HEALTH If a roommate relationship is producing sustained distress — sleep disruption, anxiety about returning to your room, fear, or any form of harassment — please contact your residence-life office or student services. You do not have to "just deal with it". Room changes are usually possible, and most institutions have processes for handling serious conflicts. Your living environment is a mental-health variable, not a test of endurance. 6.7 Romantic relationships Romantic relationships are a substantial source of both support and stress for students. A healthy relationship provides emotional regulation, practical support, a sense of being known, and a context for growth. An unhealthy one can produce sustained anxiety, depression, sleep disruption, academic decline, and, in worst cases, abuse. The fact that a relationship exists does not mean it is good for either party. What follows is not relationship advice in the broad sense — that would require its own book — but a few mental-health-relevant principles: A good relationship makes both people bigger, not smaller. If your social world, ambitions, friendships, and sense of self are shrinking around a relationship, that is a warning sign regardless of how "in love" you feel. Conflict is normal; contempt is not. The researcher John Gottman identified contempt — eye-rolling, mockery, disgust directed at the partner — as the single strongest predictor of relationship failure. Healthy couples disagree; they do not demean. Long-distance relationships can work, with structure. Explicit expectations about communication frequency, visits, and the timeline for being in the same place again substantially reduce the anxiety of distance.

Explicit expectations about communication frequency, visits, and the timeline for being in the same place again substantially reduce the anxiety of distance. Breakups are a normal part of student life and a significant mental-health event. The end of a relationship produces genuine grief, often disrupts sleep and appetite, and can trigger depressive episodes in vulnerable students. Treat a breakup as you would a major loss — with time, support, and reduced expectations of yourself for a few weeks. Abuse is never your fault, and help is available. What you are experiencing is not a relationship problem; it is a safety problem. 6.8 Social support mapping A useful exercise, adapted from social-work practice, is to map your social support network explicitly. The exercise takes fifteen minutes and often produces surprising insights about where your support is strong and where it is thin.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: YOUR SOCIAL SUPPORT MAP List the people in each of the following categories. Names only — no need to overthink. If a category is empty, leave it blank; the empty categories are the leverage points. People I could call at 3 a.m. in a crisis: People I would tell about a personal problem: People I see or speak to weekly: People I do regular activities with (study, sport, hobbies): People who challenge me to grow: People who feel safe and undemanding: Mentors, advisors, or older people I trust: Looking at your map: which categories are well-stocked, and which are thin? What is one small step you could take in the next two weeks to strengthen a thin category — joining a club, reaching out to an old friend, signing up for a mentoring programme, attending a religious or community gathering?

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 6.9 When social difficulty is more than shyness For some students, social difficulty is not a matter of habit or opportunity but of underlying social anxiety that warrants professional support. Social anxiety disorder, characterised by persistent and disproportionate fear of social judgment, is one of the most common anxiety conditions in students and is highly treatable. The student who experiences physical symptoms (racing heart, blushing, shaking, dry mouth) in social situations, who avoids classes or events because of social fear, who ruminates for hours after a social interaction about what they said wrong, may be experiencing social anxiety rather than ordinary shyness. If this resonates, please see Chapter 13 — effective support is available, and it works. Other students may be navigating social difficulty as a result of neurodivergence — autism spectrum, ADHD, or other conditions that affect social communication. For these students, the standard advice to "join a club and be more outgoing" may be unhelpful or even harmful. Finding neurodivergent-affirming social spaces, working with a therapist who understands neurodivergence, and adjusting expectations about what social connection looks like for you specifically can be far more productive than trying to fit a neurotypical mould. University disability services can help with assessment and accommodation. "You do not need to be liked by everyone. You need to be known by a few. The first is exhausting. The second is sustaining." Chapter 7 turns to the academic side of student life — the structured demands that fill most of your waking hours, and the way you meet them.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: CHAPTER 7 Academic Stress and Study-Life Balance Academic work is the central project of student life, and the way you relate to it shapes your mental health as much as the work itself does. SAFETY NOTE This chapter addresses study habits and academic stress in general. If academic stress is producing significant symptoms of depression or anxiety, or if you are considering leaving your programme for mental-health reasons, please speak with a counsellor and your academic advisor — decisions about your programme should be made with support, not in isolation. Academic stress is the most universal student experience and one of the most powerful drivers of depression and anxiety. It is also one of the most paradoxical: the same academic work that gives student life meaning and direction can, when mishandled or when amplified by perfectionism and comparison, become the primary source of suffering. This chapter is about how to do academic work in a way that protects rather than undermines your mental health — not by working less, necessarily, but by working differently. A useful starting reframe: academic stress is not a sign that you are not tough enough. It is a sign that you are attempting a demanding task under demanding conditions, with limited time, limited feedback, and high stakes. The students who appear to handle it effortlessly are, almost without exception, either managing it less well than they appear, drawing on more resources than are visible (family support, prior preparation, financial security), or running on coping strategies that will not last. The goal is not to be one of those students. The goal is to develop a sustainable relationship with academic work that you can carry into the longer career that follows.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: rces than are visible (family support, prior preparation, financial security), or running on coping strategies that will not last. The goal is not to be one of those students. The goal is to develop a sustainable relationship with academic work that you can carry into the longer career that follows. 7.1 Time management: hours versus energy Most student time-management advice focuses on hours — how to find more of them, how to allocate them efficiently, how to schedule every block. This is helpful up to a point, but it misses a more important variable: energy. An hour of academic work done when you are rested, fed, and emotionally regulated produces two to three times the output of an hour done when you are exhausted, hungry, and anxious. The student who is "working" twelve hours a day but

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: producing four hours of quality output is not actually working twelve hours; they are working four and pretending for the other eight, while depleting the recovery they need to work well the next day. The energy-aware approach to time management starts with identifying your personal peak cognitive windows — for most students, one or two periods of the day when attention, memory, and creative thinking are at their best. These windows are typically mid-morning and mid-to-late afternoon for morning types, and later in the day for evening types, but they vary considerably by individual. Once you know your windows, the principle is simple: protect your peak windows for the most cognitively demanding work, and use off-peak windows for administrative tasks, email, reading, and recovery. The single most common time-management mistake in students is spending peak cognitive windows on low-value tasks (email, social media, organising notes) and then trying to do demanding work in the evening when they are depleted. IDENTIFY YOUR PEAK WINDOW For one week, note the time of day when you find it easiest to focus on difficult material. Most students find one or two windows of two to three hours each. Protect those windows for deep work — phone off, notifications off, single task. Use the rest of the day for everything else. 7.2 Time-blocking and the Pomodoro technique Two specific techniques have strong evidence and wide adoption among students who manage academic stress well. Time-blocking is the practice of assigning specific tasks to specific time blocks in advance, rather than working from a to-do list. The advantage is that it forces realistic estimation (you cannot schedule eight hours of work in a four-hour block) and reduces the cognitive load of constant task-switching.

The advantage is that it forces realistic estimation (you cannot schedule eight hours of work in a four-hour block) and reduces the cognitive load of constant task-switching. The disadvantage is that it can become rigid and produce stress when blocks are missed; the solution is to plan with significant buffer time and to treat the schedule as a hypothesis rather than a contract. The Pomodoro technique is the practice of working in fixed short intervals — typically twenty-five minutes — separated by short breaks of five minutes, with a longer break every four intervals. The advantage is that it makes starting easier (twenty-five minutes is not intimidating), produces built-in recovery, and creates a sense of accomplishment that builds momentum. The disadvantage is that twenty-five minutes may be too short for deep creative or analytical work;

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: many students find that fifty-minute or ninety-minute blocks suit them better once they have built the habit of starting. Experiment and find what works for you. 7.3 Procrastination: not laziness, but anxiety Procrastination is one of the most misunderstood student behaviours. The popular framing — that procrastinators are lazy, undisciplined, or unmotivated — is both inaccurate and unhelpful. The research evidence points to a different explanation: procrastination is, in most cases, an emotion-regulation problem, not a time-management problem. We procrastinate not because we do not care about the task, but because thinking about the task produces negative emotions — anxiety about failure, boredom, overwhelm, self-doubt — and avoiding the task provides short-term relief from those emotions. The cost (a worse outcome later) is temporally distant; the relief (not feeling bad right now) is immediate. The brain, particularly under stress, prefers immediate relief. This reframe matters because the interventions that follow from it are different from those implied by the "laziness" framing. Telling a procrastinator to "just be more disciplined" is like telling an anxious person to "just calm down" — it identifies the right outcome but offers no useful mechanism. The interventions that actually work target the emotional resistance, not the discipline. SPECIFIC ANTI-PROCRASTINATION PRACTICES Make the first step absurdly small. "Write the essay" is paralysing. "Open the document and write one sentence" is achievable. Once you have started, momentum usually carries you further. The hurdle is almost always the start, not the continuation. Lower your standards for the first draft.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: PRACTICES Make the first step absurdly small. "Write the essay" is paralysing. "Open the document and write one sentence" is achievable. Once you have started, momentum usually carries you further. The hurdle is almost always the start, not the continuation. Lower your standards for the first draft. Perfectionism drives procrastination; the harder you try to make the first draft, the harder it is to start. Give yourself explicit permission to write badly at first. You can edit bad writing; you cannot edit no writing. Name the emotion. When you notice yourself avoiding a task, pause and ask: what am I feeling? Often the answer is fear — of failure, of judgment, of not being good enough. Naming the fear reduces its power, and opens the possibility of addressing it directly rather than running from it. Use implementation intentions. "I will study this afternoon" is vague and easily deferred. "I will sit down at my desk at 2 p.m. and read the first ten pages of chapter four" is specific and harder to escape. The formula is: When [situation], I will [specific action].

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Reduce friction. If you procrastinate on going to the library, pack your bag the night before and put it by the door. If you procrastinate on opening your laptop, close all distracting tabs the night before. If you procrastinate on writing, leave the document open with a half-finished sentence from yesterday. Forgive yourself for past procrastination. Students who beat themselves up for procrastinating procrastinate more, not less — the self-criticism adds to the negative emotion that drives the avoidance in the first place. Acknowledge the pattern, gently redirect, and move on. 7.4 Perfectionism: when high standards become a vulnerability Perfectionism was introduced in Chapter 2 as a specific risk factor for depression and anxiety. Here we look at how it operates in academic life and what to do about it. Perfectionism is not the same as having high standards or caring about quality. It is a specific combination of unrealistically high standards, conditional self-worth ("I am only valuable if I achieve at this level"), harsh self-criticism when standards are not met, and fear of failure that drives both overwork and avoidance. The academic environment reinforces perfectionism at every turn. Grades are visible and rank-ordered. Competitive programmes select for it. Employers and graduate schools reward it. Parents and peers praise it. The result is that many high-achieving students arrive at university with perfectionism so deeply embedded that it feels like a personality trait rather than a coping strategy — and one that appears to be working, because it produces high grades. The cost — anxiety, procrastination, brittle self-esteem, exhaustion, eating disorders, and, eventually, burnout — is less visible but accumulates over years.

The cost — anxiety, procrastination, brittle self-esteem, exhaustion, eating disorders, and, eventually, burnout — is less visible but accumulates over years. The evidence-based interventions for perfectionism target each of its components. Standards can be revised by setting explicit "good enough" criteria for each task: what would a competent, non-perfectionist version of this work look like? Aim for that, not for the impossible ideal. Conditional self-worth can be loosened by deliberately cultivating sources of value outside achievement — relationships, hobbies, character, contribution. Self-criticism can be replaced with self-compassion (see Chapter 10). Fear of failure can be reduced by exposure: deliberately attempting things you might fail at, in low-stakes contexts, to recalibrate the brain's threat response to failure.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: THE 80/20 REFRAME In most academic work, 80 percent of the value is produced by 20 percent of the effort — and the remaining 20 percent of the value requires 80 percent of the effort. The perfectionist student spends the last 80 percent polishing work that is already good enough, leaving no time or energy for the next task. The sustainable student identifies the 80-percent-quality point, stops there, and moves on. Your grades may differ slightly. Your mental health, your sustainability, and your capacity to take on more interesting work will differ enormously. 7.5 Exam anxiety Exam anxiety is a specific form of performance anxiety that affects a large proportion of students and that, paradoxically, tends to lower the performance it threatens. The student who has studied thoroughly but "freezes" in the exam is not underprepared; they are overactivated. Their sympathetic nervous system has shifted into a fight-or-flight state that impairs the very cognitive functions — working memory, flexible retrieval, sustained attention — that the exam requires. The interventions for exam anxiety fall into three categories. Preparation matters, but only up to a point — beyond a certain level of preparation, additional study does not reduce anxiety and may increase it. Cognitive techniques include reframing the physiological arousal (a racing heart is energy, not catastrophe), challenging catastrophic predictions ("I will fail and my life is over"), and using self-compassion to interrupt the self-critical inner voice. Somatic techniques include slow diaphragmatic breathing (which directly activates the parasympathetic nervous system), grounding exercises (the 5-43-2-1 sensory exercise, described in Chapter 10), and progressive muscle relaxation.

Behavioural techniques include deliberate exposure to exam-like conditions (taking timed practice exams under realistic conditions) and developing a pre-exam routine that signals safety to the nervous system. For students whose exam anxiety is severe enough to impair performance despite preparation, formal accommodations (extra time, a quiet room, breaks) may be available through disability services. Exam anxiety that rises to the level of a panic disorder is a treatable condition; please see Chapter 13 if this resonates.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 7.6 Asking for extensions and accommodations Many students endure significant academic stress because they are reluctant to ask for extensions or accommodations, even when they are entitled to them and even when asking would substantially improve their outcome. The reluctance is understandable — it feels like an admission of failure, a burden on the professor, a mark of being "less than" — but it is, in most cases, unnecessary. Most professors and institutions would far rather know early that you are struggling and adjust accordingly than discover at the end of the term that you have fallen behind irretrievably. The mechanics of asking are simpler than students often imagine. A brief, factual email — "I have been dealing with a health issue this week and would like to request a 48-hour extension on the assignment due Friday. I have attached a doctor's note / I can provide documentation if needed. Thank you for your consideration." — is usually sufficient. Most institutions also have formal processes for medical or compassionate extensions, and most have disability accommodation processes for students with documented conditions (including mental-health conditions). Your university's student services or disability office can walk you through what is available. A REFRAME WORTH INTERNALISING Asking for an extension is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign that you understand your own capacity and are managing your work accordingly — which is a skill employers and graduate programmes actively value. The student who silently misses a deadline because they could not bring themselves to ask for help is not more impressive than the student who asks early and delivers good work slightly later.

The line is crossed when the stress starts affecting sleep, appetite, mood, concentration, social functioning, or sense of self over weeks rather than days. If you notice the following patterns, please take them seriously: Inability to stop thinking about academic work, even during rest, social activities, or attempts to relax Sleep consistently disrupted by academic worry — either unable to fall asleep, or waking in the early hours with racing thoughts

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Persistent physical symptoms — headaches, stomach-aches, chest tightness, muscle tension — that track with academic demands Avoidance of academic work that has moved from occasional procrastination to a paralysing pattern Sense of dread about going to class, opening your laptop, or checking email Loss of interest in subjects or activities you previously enjoyed Thoughts of giving up, dropping out, or escaping that feel more urgent than considered Increased use of alcohol or other substances to manage academic stress None of these mean you are weak or unfit for your programme. They mean the system is overloaded and needs recalibration — which may involve reducing load, seeking accommodation, getting professional support, or, in some cases, taking a leave of absence. These are legitimate options, not failures. Many students who take a reduced load or a leave return to complete their programmes with better outcomes than if they had pushed through. 7.8 Comparison with peers Academic environments are comparison machines. You see other students' grades, other students' contributions in class, other students' opportunities, other students' social lives (curated, on social media). The natural conclusion — "everyone is doing better than me" — is almost always false, but it feels true because you are comparing your inside (your doubts, your struggles, your unfinished work) to other people's outside (their visible accomplishments, their composed presentations, their finished products). The antidote to comparison is not to stop comparing — the brain does it automatically — but to compare differently.

The antidote to comparison is not to stop comparing — the brain does it automatically — but to compare differently. Compare to your past self, not to other people: am I making progress on the things that matter to me? Compare full contexts, not curated snapshots: the student who appears to be thriving may be struggling in ways you cannot see. Compare on dimensions you actually value, not on dimensions the environment happens to make visible. And, where possible, reduce the comparison input — unfollow social media accounts that produce comparison, limit time in environments that activate comparison, and spend more time with people who see you as a whole person rather than as a competitor.

The second is corrosive." 7.9 Sustainable study habits: a summary Bringing the pieces together, the student who manages academic stress sustainably tends to do the following: Protects their peak cognitive windows for deep work, and uses off-peak windows for everything else Uses some form of time-blocking or Pomodoro to structure work sessions Treats starting as the main problem, and makes first steps absurdly small Writes bad first drafts and edits them, rather than trying to write perfect first drafts Sets explicit "good enough" criteria and stops there Asks for extensions or accommodations early rather than late Builds in recovery — sleep, movement, social time — as a non-negotiable part of the schedule, not as what gets cut when work piles up Reduces comparison input where possible Treats academic stress that produces sustained symptoms as a mental-health issue, not a study-skills issue Chapter 8 turns to a stressor that is often invisible in student mental-health discussions but that drives a large share of the actual distress: money, and the basic needs it secures.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: CHAPTER 8 Financial Wellness and Basic Needs Money is one of the most powerful and least discussed determinants of student mental health. Naming it clearly is the first step toward managing it. SAFETY NOTE This chapter addresses financial stress in general terms and signposts sources of support. It does not provide financial advice, debt counselling, or benefit eligibility assessment. For specific guidance, please consult your institution's financial aid office or a qualified advisor. Financial stress is one of the strongest predictors of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation in student populations — in many studies, stronger than academic stress or social isolation. It is also one of the most under-discussed. Money carries a particular shame in many cultures, and students who are struggling financially often hide it from peers, mentors, and even family. This hiding deepens isolation, prevents access to support, and turns a difficult situation into a private catastrophe. This chapter aims to put financial stress on the table as a normal, common, and addressable student experience — not by minimising it, but by clarifying what it is, why it matters, and what helps. 8.1 Why financial stress hits students hard Student financial stress is structurally different from adult financial stress in several ways. First, students typically have low or zero income relative to their living costs, and what income they have is often irregular (part-time work, gig work, family contributions that vary month to month). Second, students face large fixed costs — tuition, rent, textbooks, transport — that cannot be reduced without major life changes.

Second, students face large fixed costs — tuition, rent, textbooks, transport — that cannot be reduced without major life changes. Third, students often have limited financial literacy and limited experience managing budgets independently, which makes the cognitive load of financial management higher than it will be later in life. Fourth, students are often financially dependent on family in ways that complicate autonomy — decisions about majors, careers, and even social life may be shaped by family financial expectations. Fifth, the stakes feel existential: dropping out, taking on debt, or failing to convert the degree into a job feel like life-defining failures rather than reversible setbacks.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: The mental-health impact runs through several pathways. The direct pathway is the chronic activation of the stress response produced by financial precarity — the constant low-grade alertness of "will I have enough this month", which elevates cortisol, disrupts sleep, and produces anxiety. The indirect pathway is the way financial stress forces compromises on every other protective factor: students who work long hours to afford rent have less time for sleep, movement, social connection, and recovery; students who cannot afford nutritious food eat poorly and feel worse; students who cannot afford social activities withdraw and become lonely; students who cannot afford counselling do not get counselling. The cognitive pathway is "scarcity mindset" — the well-documented finding that financial stress consumes cognitive bandwidth, reducing capacity for planning, decision-making, and self-regulation. The student who seems to be making "bad decisions" about money, academics, or self-care may simply be operating with a depleted cognitive budget. 8.2 Food insecurity: a hidden crisis Among the most under-recognised student stressors is food insecurity — limited or uncertain availability of nutritionally adequate and safe food. Surveys in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and elsewhere consistently find that between 20 and 40 percent of students at four-year institutions experience some level of food insecurity in a given year. The figure is higher at community colleges and among first-generation students, students of colour, students with dependents, and LGBTQ+ students. Food insecurity is associated with depression, anxiety, lower GPA, higher rates of dropout, and poorer sleep.

It is not a "lifestyle" issue or a matter of being thrifty; it is a basic-needs failure with direct mental-health consequences. A student who is skipping meals to afford rent, who is eating the cheapest possible food regardless of nutritional value, or who is uncertain where the next meal will come from is operating under a level of physiological stress that makes every other task harder. 1 in 3 Students at four-year institutions experience some level of food insecurity in a given year. The figure is higher at community colleges and among first-generation students, students of colour, and student-parents.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 8.3 What support exists (and how to find it) Many students who are struggling financially are unaware of the support that exists on their campus and in their community. The following are commonly available, though specifics vary by institution and country: Campus food pantries and basic-needs centres. Many universities now operate food pantries, free meal programmes, or basic-needs centres that provide food, toiletries, and other essentials at no cost and with minimal paperwork. These are typically run by student affairs or student services. Emergency aid funds. Most institutions have emergency funds for students facing sudden financial crises (loss of housing, medical bills, family emergency). These are usually one-time grants, not loans, and do not require repayment. The application is typically short and decisions are fast. Government benefits. Depending on your country and circumstances, you may be eligible for food assistance (SNAP in the US, equivalent programmes elsewhere), housing support, healthcare subsidies, or income support. Eligibility rules for students are often complex; a benefits counsellor or basicneeds navigator can help. Scholarships and bursaries. Beyond the major scholarships awarded at admission, many institutions have smaller bursaries and emergency scholarships that are under-claimed. Your financial aid office can tell you what is available. Fee waivers and payment plans. If you cannot pay tuition or fees on time, contact the financial aid office before the deadline. Many institutions can defer payment, set up instalment plans, or waive late fees. Silence is the worst option; communication usually produces options. Work-study and on-campus employment.

Silence is the worst option; communication usually produces options. Work-study and on-campus employment. On-campus jobs often pay better than off-campus equivalents, have more flexible scheduling around classes, and may be reserved for students with financial need. Childcare support. For student-parents, many institutions have childcare subsidies, family housing, or partnerships with local childcare providers. Basic-needs navigators. Even if your institution does not have a formal navigator, student services can usually direct you.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: A REFRAME ON ASKING The shame associated with accessing food pantries, emergency aid, or benefits is real, and it is the main reason students go without support they are entitled to. The reframe worth internalising: these programmes exist because student financial stress is common and structural, not because individual students have failed. Using them is not taking from others; it is using resources that were created for exactly your situation. If you are eligible, please use them. If you are not sure whether you are eligible, please ask. 8.4 Budgeting that reduces cognitive load The goal of student budgeting is not to optimise every dollar; it is to reduce the cognitive load of constant financial decision-making. A budget that you actually use is far better than an ideal budget that you abandon after two weeks. The following principles, drawn from behavioural economics, make budgeting more sustainable: Automate what you can. Automated payments for rent, utilities, and savings eliminate decision-making and reduce the risk of late fees. Use categories, not line items. Three categories — fixed costs (rent, tuition, transport), food, and everything else — are usually enough. Detailed line-item budgets are abandoned quickly. Track after the fact, not before. Spending five minutes a week reviewing what you actually spent is more sustainable than planning every purchase in advance. Many banking apps now do this automatically. Build a small buffer. Even a tiny emergency fund — a month's rent, say — substantially reduces the cognitive load of financial precarity. Build it slowly; do not let the goal of an "ideal" emergency fund prevent you from starting. Plan for irregular costs.

Build it slowly; do not let the goal of an "ideal" emergency fund prevent you from starting. Plan for irregular costs. Textbooks at the start of term, travel home for holidays, deposits on new housing — these are predictable but irregular. Setting aside a small amount monthly for them prevents the shock when they arrive. Be honest about what you can and cannot afford. The most expensive financial decision many students make is trying to maintain a social life that exceeds their budget. Honest conversations with friends about what you can afford — and choosing friends who make those conversations easy — are a form of financial self-protection.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 8.5 Work and study: balancing income and academic load Many students work during term. For some, work is a financial necessity; for others, a way to gain experience or reduce debt. The relationship between work and academic outcomes is not linear — students who work a moderate amount (10 to 15 hours per week) often do as well academically as students who do not work at all, and may develop time-management skills that non-working students do not. Students who work more than 20 hours per week, however, tend to show lower grades, more stress, and higher rates of mental-health problems. The trade-off is not always avoidable — financial necessity may require more than 20 hours — but it is worth knowing where the threshold lies. If you must work significant hours, the following can help protect your academic and mental health: prioritise on-campus or work-study jobs that accommodate your class schedule; choose jobs with predictable hours rather than gig work that can be called up at any time; build your class schedule around your work commitments rather than the reverse where possible; talk to your academic advisor about reducing your course load if necessary; and treat your sleep as non-negotiable, even if it means earning slightly less. 8.6 Debt and the future-self problem For many students, taking on debt is unavoidable and is, in itself, a rational investment in future earnings and life options. The mental-health impact of student debt is not primarily about the absolute amount; it is about the relationship the student has with the debt — whether it feels like an investment in a manageable future or like an unpayable burden that will define the next twenty years. Useful reframes: debt is a tool, not a moral failing.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: f student debt is not primarily about the absolute amount; it is about the relationship the student has with the debt — whether it feels like an investment in a manageable future or like an unpayable burden that will define the next twenty years. Useful reframes: debt is a tool, not a moral failing. Student loans are typically structured to be repaid gradually after graduation, often with income-based repayment options that cap payments at a percentage of income. The presence of debt does not mean you have failed; it means you have accessed education through a mechanism that the system is designed around. Focus on what you can control — completing your programme, building employable skills, and making informed choices about further borrowing — rather than on the total debt figure, which can feel paralysing. Talk to a financial aid counsellor if you are struggling; they can often help with repayment planning, consolidation, or relief options you may not know about.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 8.7 The shame around money Money shame is one of the most powerful and least visible forces in student mental health. Students who grew up with less than their peers may feel embarrassed about what they cannot afford, where they live, what they eat, what they wear, and what they cannot participate in. Students who grew up with more may feel guilty about what they have, or pressure to maintain a lifestyle they cannot independently afford. Students who are financially dependent on families with expectations may feel that their choices are not their own. International students may be navigating exchange rates, family expectations, and visa restrictions that compound the stress. The antidote to money shame is not disclosure for its own sake — you do not owe anyone the details of your finances. It is finding, in your life, one or two people with whom you can be honest about money. A trusted friend, a partner, a sibling, a mentor, a counsellor — someone who knows what your actual situation is and with whom you do not have to perform. The performance of financial normalcy is itself exhausting, and dropping it with even one person can substantially reduce the cognitive load. "Money is not a personal failing or a personal virtue. It is a structural condition. Treating it as the first rather than the second is most of what financial wellness actually means." 8.8 When financial stress is producing symptoms If financial stress is producing sustained depression or anxiety symptoms — sleep disruption, persistent worry, panic attacks, hopelessness, intrusive thoughts — please treat it as the mental-health issue it is, not as a financial issue you should solve alone.

University counselling services are familiar with financial stress and can help, both directly (with the emotional impact) and indirectly (by connecting you to financial support you may not know about). Chapter 9 turns to a stressor that is genuinely new to your generation, and that interacts with almost every other factor in this guide: the digital environment.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: CHAPTER 9 Digital Well-being Your phone is not the enemy of your mental health. But your relationship with it almost certainly matters more than you think. SAFETY NOTE This chapter addresses general digital well-being. If you are experiencing online harassment, stalking, or image-based abuse, please contact your campus safety office or a specialised helpline (see Chapter 15) — these are safety issues, not lifestyle issues. No factor has reshaped student mental health in the last fifteen years as much as the arrival of the always-on smartphone and the social-media ecosystem it enables. This chapter takes a deliberately measured stance: the technology is not going away, and most of the moral panic about it is overblown, but the way it is designed and the way most students use it produces measurable effects on attention, sleep, mood, social comparison, and identity formation. The goal is not to abandon the tools — they are genuinely useful — but to use them on your terms rather than on the terms of the attention-extraction industry that built them. 9.1 What the evidence actually says The research on screens and adolescent/young-adult mental health is large, contested, and often oversimplified in popular coverage. The honest summary is roughly as follows. Total screen time is a poor predictor of mental-health outcomes; the relationship is weak and disappears entirely when content and context are accounted for. Active use (messaging friends, creating content, participating in communities) is generally associated with neutral or positive mental-health outcomes. Passive use (endless scrolling of feeds, consuming content without interaction) is associated with negative outcomes.

text: and context are accounted for. Active use (messaging friends, creating content, participating in communities) is generally associated with neutral or positive mental-health outcomes. Passive use (endless scrolling of feeds, consuming content without interaction) is associated with negative outcomes. Social comparison use (looking at peers' curated lives and comparing to your own) is the most consistently negative pattern, particularly for young women. Bedtime use is consistently negative, through both light exposure (see Chapter 4) and emotional activation. Use during academic work consistently impairs performance, even when the user believes they are multitasking effectively.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: The effect sizes are not catastrophic for most students, but they are real, and they compound. A student whose sleep is shortened by an hour of late-night scrolling, whose attention is fragmented by constant notifications, whose selfimage is shaped by exposure to idealised peers, and whose social confidence is undermined by parasitic online relationships is accumulating a meaningful mental-health cost. The cost is rarely large enough to be the "cause" of depression or anxiety on its own, but it is large enough to shift the baseline. 9.2 The four big problems 1. ATTENTION FRAGMENTATION The brain cannot truly multitask; it switches, and switching has a cost. Every notification, every check of the phone, every context shift between work and message and feed produces a small attentional residue that reduces the quality of the next task. The student who checks their phone every five minutes while studying is not studying — they are performing a low-quality version of studying interleaved with high-quality distraction. Research suggests that even the presence of a phone in view — not being used, just visible — reduces cognitive capacity, because the brain is devoting attention to suppressing the urge to check it. 2. SLEEP DISRUPTION Covered in detail in Chapter 4. The two mechanisms — light exposure and emotional activation — combine to make bedtime phone use one of the most reliably disruptive habits in student life. The student who cannot sleep without their phone is, in many cases, not sleeping because of their phone. 3. SOCIAL COMPARISON Social media platforms are comparison engines.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: posure and emotional activation — combine to make bedtime phone use one of the most reliably disruptive habits in student life. The student who cannot sleep without their phone is, in many cases, not sleeping because of their phone. 3. SOCIAL COMPARISON Social media platforms are comparison engines. They are designed to surface the most engaging content, which is typically the most idealised version of other people's lives — their best photos, their biggest achievements, their most curated moments. The brain has no built-in correction for this; it treats the curated feed as representative of the person's actual life, and concludes that everyone else is doing better than you. This is the "compare your inside to other people's outside" problem, amplified to industrial scale. The comparison effect is strongest for the content most relevant to your life stage: peers' academic achievements, social lives, romantic relationships, body images, travel, and career moves. The students most vulnerable to comparisondriven distress are those whose self-esteem is already contingent on external

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: validation, those in competitive academic environments, and those in the early stages of major life transitions (first year, final year, post-graduation) when comparison feels most consequential. 4. PARASOCIAL SUBSTITUTION A "parasocial relationship" is a one-sided relationship with a media figure — a YouTuber, a streamer, an influencer, a celebrity. These relationships can be genuinely meaningful and are not inherently problematic. But when they substitute for, rather than supplement, real-world relationships, they leave the user feeling both stimulated and lonely — the worst combination. The student who spends three hours a day with a favourite streamer and zero hours with real friends is filling time without filling the belonging need, which produces a particular kind of emptiness that is hard to name but easy to feel. 9.3 What helps: practical interventions The evidence on digital-well-being interventions is mixed — many interventions produce small, short-lived effects because the underlying design of the platforms is unchanged. But the following practices have shown reasonably consistent benefits and are worth trying: Move your phone charger out of the bedroom The single most effective digital well-being intervention. Removes bedtime use, removes the morning scroll, removes the sleep-onset disruption. Use a separate alarm clock. Most students who try this for two weeks report meaningful sleep improvements. Turn off non-essential notifications Most apps default to notifying you about everything, because engagement is their business model. Turn off notifications for everything except messages from actual humans, calendar reminders, and alarms. You will check apps when you choose to, not when they summon you.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Use grey scale Setting your phone screen to grey scale (in accessibility settings) removes the rewarding colour stimulation that makes apps addictive. Many users find that scrolling loses its pull within days. Try it for a week. Curate your feeds aggressively Unfollow accounts that produce comparison, anxiety, or selfloathing — even accounts you "like". Follow accounts that produce genuine interest, learning, or connection. The feed is shaped by your behaviour; you can teach it to serve you better. Schedule offline blocks Particular times of day — first hour after waking, the hour before bed, during meals with others, during deep work — are highleverage times to be offline. Treat them as protected. Use one screen at a time Watching a film while scrolling your phone produces a worse experience of both. Single-tasking your leisure — giving the film, the book, the conversation your full attention — produces more rest and more pleasure than the divided version. 9.4 Social media specifically Social media deserves specific attention because it is the category most consistently associated with student mental-health problems. The platforms differ — Instagram and TikTok are more comparison-driven; Twitter/X is more outrage-driven; messaging apps are more genuinely social; Reddit and Discord communities can be either, depending on use — but a few general principles apply across platforms. Notice your mood before and after use. If a particular platform consistently leaves you feeling worse — more anxious, more envious, more hopeless, more irritated — that is information. The platform is not neutral for you, regardless of how neutral it is for others. You do not need a reason to reduce or leave a platform that is making you worse. Distinguish active from passive use.

You do not need a reason to reduce or leave a platform that is making you worse. Distinguish active from passive use. Messaging a friend, commenting on a post you care about, sharing something you made — these are active uses and are generally fine. Scrolling a feed for forty minutes without interacting is

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: passive use and is generally the most damaging pattern. If you cannot avoid the passive use, consider removing the app from your phone and accessing it only on a desktop, where the friction naturally limits the use. Be honest about why you are using it. Often, the reach for the phone is not about information or connection; it is about escaping an uncomfortable feeling — boredom, anxiety, loneliness, the difficulty of starting a task. The phone is a highly effective feeling-escape device, which is precisely why it is so hard to put down. Building other, less costly ways to manage those feelings — a short walk, a few breaths, a glass of water, a text to a friend — gives you options beyond the phone. 9.5 News, doomscrolling, and information overload A particular digital pattern that has intensified in recent years is "doomscrolling" — the compulsive consumption of negative news, often late at night, often past the point of any informational value. The pattern is driven by the brain's threatdetection system: in uncertain times, monitoring for threats feels adaptive, even when the monitoring cannot meaningfully reduce the threat. The result is a state of sustained low-grade activation that disrupts sleep, elevates anxiety, and produces a sense of helplessness about the state of the world. The antidote is not ignorance — staying informed matters — but bounded information consumption. Specific times of day, specific sources, specific duration. Avoiding news in the hour before bed. Avoiding breaking-news alerts that pull attention at all hours. Recognising that for almost any event of genuine consequence, you will hear about it through other channels even if you are not actively monitoring.

text: imes of day, specific sources, specific duration. Avoiding news in the hour before bed. Avoiding breaking-news alerts that pull attention at all hours. Recognising that for almost any event of genuine consequence, you will hear about it through other channels even if you are not actively monitoring. The student who checks the news twice a day, for fifteen minutes each time, is as well-informed as the student who monitors it continuously, and substantially less anxious. 9.6 Online communities: genuine belonging or substitute? Online communities — Discord servers, Reddit forums, Facebook groups, gaming clans — can be genuine sources of belonging, particularly for students whose offline options are limited (international students, students in isolated locations, students with niche interests, LGBTQ+ students in unsupportive environments, neurodivergent students). The relationships formed in these communities can be real, deep, and enduring. They are not inherently inferior to offline relationships.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: That said, online communities have specific risks. They can become echo chambers that reinforce unhelpful beliefs (including, in some communities, beliefs that worsen depression or anxiety). They can expose users to harmful content, including pro-eating-disorder, pro-self-harm, or extremist material. They can substitute for offline relationships in ways that leave the user more isolated over time, not less. And they can be contexts for harassment, exploitation, and grooming, particularly of vulnerable users. The principles for healthy online community use: be selective about which communities you join; pay attention to how they make you feel; maintain at least some offline relationships alongside online ones; be cautious about disclosing personal information; and if a community is producing harm rather than support, leave it. The internet is large; better communities exist. "Your phone is a tool. Use it when it serves you. Put it down when it does not. The hard part is not the putting down — it is noticing when it has stopped serving you." Chapter 10 turns to a set of practices that have travelled from clinical and contemplative traditions into mainstream student life: mindfulness, selfcompassion, and other coping skills that you can use in real time. CHAPTER 10 Mindfulness, Self-Compassion, and Coping Skills A toolkit of small, evidence-based practices you can use in real time — not as therapy, but as the everyday mental equivalent of stretching, drinking water, and taking deep breaths. SAFETY NOTE The practices in this chapter are framed as self-care, not as therapy. They are not a substitute for professional support, and they are not appropriate as the only intervention for significant depression or anxiety.

They are not a substitute for professional support, and they are not appropriate as the only intervention for significant depression or anxiety. If you have a trauma history, please approach meditation practices with care — some can be activating rather than calming, and a trauma-informed therapist can help you find what works for you.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: This chapter gathers a set of practices that the research literature consistently finds helpful for student mental health, and that have the advantage of being free, portable, and usable in real time. None of them is a cure. None of them replaces sleep, social connection, or professional support when needed. What they offer is a set of small tools for managing the everyday texture of stress — the moment of panic before a presentation, the rumination spiral at 2 a.m., the self-critical loop after a difficult conversation, the overwhelm of a stack of deadlines. Used regularly, they accumulate into a greater capacity to stay present with difficult experience rather than being swept away by it. 10.1 What mindfulness is (and is not) Mindfulness, as defined by the researcher Jon Kabat-Zinn who did most to bring it into mainstream medicine, is "the awareness that arises from paying attention, on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgmentally". It is not a religion, despite its Buddhist origins. It is not relaxation, though it can be relaxing. It is not emptying the mind of thoughts, which is impossible. It is not positive thinking, which is a different (and often less helpful) practice. It is the simple — though not easy — act of noticing what is happening right now, with acceptance rather than resistance. The relevance to student mental health is direct. Much of the suffering in anxiety and depression is not in the present moment itself, which is often bearable, but in the brain's departure from it — into future worries ("what if I fail the exam?"), past ruminations ("why did I say that?"), or self-referential narratives ("I am a failure").

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: direct. Much of the suffering in anxiety and depression is not in the present moment itself, which is often bearable, but in the brain's departure from it — into future worries ("what if I fail the exam?"), past ruminations ("why did I say that?"), or self-referential narratives ("I am a failure"). These departures are not just thoughts; they are full physiological events that activate the stress response, raise cortisol, and produce real changes in mood and body. The capacity to notice the departure and return to the present interrupts the spiral before it amplifies. This is a skill, not a trait, and it can be developed through practice. 10.2 Brief breathing practices The breath is the most accessible lever for regulating the nervous system in real time. Unlike thoughts, which can be difficult to direct, the breath can be consciously controlled, and changes in breathing pattern produce rapid changes in heart rate, blood pressure, and autonomic nervous system activity. The following practices are simple, evidence-based, and effective for most students.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: BOX BREATHING (4-4-4-4) Used by military personnel and emergency responders to regulate arousal under pressure. Inhale for four counts, hold for four counts, exhale for four counts, hold for four counts. Repeat for two to five minutes. Useful before stressful events (exams, presentations, difficult conversations) and during acute anxiety. PHYSIOLOGICAL SIGH (DOUBLE INHALE, LONG EXHALE) The fastest evidence-based way to reduce acute anxiety. Two short inhales through the nose (the second one stacking on top of the first), followed by a long slow exhale through the mouth. Repeat three to five times. Works by opening collapsed alveoli in the lungs and slowing the heart rate via the vagus nerve. Useful in the moment of acute stress — before a presentation, during a panic attack, after receiving bad news. 4-7-8 BREATHING Inhale through the nose for four counts, hold for seven counts, exhale through the mouth for eight counts. The long exhale activates the parasympathetic nervous system. Useful for falling asleep and for general anxiety reduction. Four cycles is usually enough; do not overdo it, as it can produce light-headedness. THREE MINDFUL BREATHS The shortest practice. Pause, take one full breath with attention on the sensation of the air entering and leaving the body, then two more. Takes less than thirty seconds. Useful as a transition between activities — between classes, between work and rest, between waking and reaching for the phone. 10.3 Grounding: the 5-4-3-2-1 exercise When the mind is racing or dissociating, grounding exercises bring attention back to the body and the present moment. The 5-4-3-2-1 exercise is the most widely taught:

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 5-4-3-2-1 GROUNDING Look around and name (silently or aloud): 5 things you can see — describe each briefly 4 things you can physically feel — the chair, your feet on the floor, the texture of your clothes 3 things you can hear — distant and nearby sounds 2 things you can smell — or two of your favourite smells 1 thing you can taste — or one thing you like about yourself The exercise takes two to three minutes and reliably reduces acute anxiety by anchoring attention in sensory present-moment experience. 10.4 Body scan and progressive muscle relaxation The body scan is a mindfulness practice in which you move attention slowly through the body, from feet to head or head to feet, noticing sensations in each region without trying to change them. It is particularly useful for students who live mostly in their heads and have lost contact with bodily sensation. The practice takes ten to twenty minutes and can be done lying down before sleep (in which case it often becomes a sleep aid) or sitting during a break. Many free guided versions are available online. Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) is a related practice in which you systematically tense and then release each muscle group in the body. It is particularly useful for students who carry physical tension — in the jaw, shoulders, stomach, or hands — that they may not even be aware of until they release it. PMR takes fifteen to twenty minutes and is often done in the evening. It is one of the most evidence-based relaxation practices for anxiety and insomnia. 10.5 Self-compassion practices Self-compassion, introduced in Chapter 3 as a protective factor, can be deliberately cultivated through brief structured practices.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: n to twenty minutes and is often done in the evening. It is one of the most evidence-based relaxation practices for anxiety and insomnia. 10.5 Self-compassion practices Self-compassion, introduced in Chapter 3 as a protective factor, can be deliberately cultivated through brief structured practices. The researcher Kristin Neff describes three core practices: THE SELF-COMPASSION BREAK A short practice for difficult moments. When you notice you are struggling — you have made a mistake, received a setback, or are feeling inadequate — pause and say to yourself (silently or aloud):

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: THE THREE PHRASES 1. Mindfulness: "This is a moment of suffering" (or "This is hard right now" — naming the difficulty without dramatising or minimising it). 2. Common humanity: "Suffering is part of life" (or "Other people feel this way too" — recognising that struggle is human, not a personal failure). 3. Self-kindness: "May I be kind to myself in this moment" (or "May I give myself the compassion I need" — offering yourself the warmth you would offer a friend). The whole practice takes less than a minute. Used consistently, it interrupts the self-critical spiral and builds the capacity to respond to difficulty with care rather than attack. THE FRIEND REFRAME When you notice you are being harsh with yourself about a mistake or shortcoming, pause and ask: what would I say to a good friend who came to me with this exact situation? Then say that to yourself. Most students find that the words they would offer a friend are dramatically warmer and more reasonable than the words they are giving themselves. The point is not to lie to yourself or lower your standards; it is to apply the same compassion to yourself that you would extend to someone you care about. SELF-COMPASSION JOURNALING A brief evening practice: write down one thing that was difficult during the day, one way you struggled with it, and one kind thing you could say to yourself about it. Takes five minutes. Research shows that doing this daily for two weeks produces measurable increases in self-compassion and reductions in selfcriticism. 10.6 Journaling Journaling is one of the most evidence-based writing practices for mental health.
