text: ne kind thing you could say to yourself about it. Takes five minutes. Research shows that doing this daily for two weeks produces measurable increases in self-compassion and reductions in selfcriticism. 10.6 Journaling Journaling is one of the most evidence-based writing practices for mental health. The forms that work best for student distress are slightly different from the "dear diary" model and worth distinguishing: EXPRESSIVE WRITING Developed by the psychologist James Pennebaker. The practice: write continuously for fifteen to twenty minutes, for three or four consecutive days, about a difficult emotional experience — something you have not fully processed. The instruction is to write about your deepest thoughts and feelings,

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: without worrying about grammar, spelling, or what anyone else would think. The mechanism appears to be the construction of a coherent narrative around an experience that was previously held as fragmented emotional memory, which reduces its intrusive quality. The evidence base is substantial, with benefits shown for mood, immune function, and even academic performance. GRATITUDE JOURNALING Each evening, write down three things you are grateful for from the day. The items can be small (a good cup of coffee, a moment of sunlight, a kind word from a stranger). The mechanism is the redirection of attention toward what is going well, which counters the negativity bias that depression and anxiety produce. Benefits are shown with as little as two weeks of practice, though the effect is stronger when the practice is sustained. The gratitude should be genuine, not performed; if you cannot find three things, find one. WORRY JOURNALING A dedicated time and place for worries. Each evening (or whenever worries are interfering with sleep or focus), write down everything you are worried about. The act of externalising the worries reduces their hold on working memory. For each worry, note: is this something I can act on? If yes, what is one small step? If no, can I let it go for tonight? The practice converts amorphous anxiety into specific concerns, many of which turn out to be more manageable than they felt. STREAM-OF-CONSCIOUSNESS JOURNALING Write continuously for a set period (five to fifteen minutes) about whatever comes to mind, without editing or directing. Useful for clearing the mind, processing the day, and noticing patterns over time. Less structured than expressive writing, but more sustainable as a daily practice.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: S JOURNALING Write continuously for a set period (five to fifteen minutes) about whatever comes to mind, without editing or directing. Useful for clearing the mind, processing the day, and noticing patterns over time. Less structured than expressive writing, but more sustainable as a daily practice. 10.7 Cognitive reframing (lightly) The cognitive-behavioural tradition offers a range of techniques for working with unhelpful thought patterns. This guide is not the place for a full CBT manual, but one technique — cognitive reframing — is portable enough to be worth introducing. The practice: when you notice a distressing thought, pause and ask four questions:

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: THE FOUR QUESTIONS 1. Is this thought true? (What is the evidence for and against it?) 2. Is this thought helpful? (Even if it were true, is dwelling on it helping me?) 3. What would I say to a friend who had this thought? 4. Is there another way to see this? (What alternative interpretation fits the same facts?) The point is not to convince yourself that everything is fine. It is to loosen the grip of a single interpretation, which creates space for a more workable one. This is a self-care practice, not a substitute for the structured cognitive work that a therapist would guide. 10.8 Values clarification Depression and anxiety often produce a narrowing of attention onto immediate threats and discomforts, at the cost of contact with what actually matters to you. Values clarification is a brief practice for reconnecting with the larger direction of your life. The exercise: take ten minutes and write down your answers to the following questions.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: VALUES CLARIFICATION 1. What do you want your life to be about? (Not what you want to do — what you want to stand for.) 2. If you were at your eighty-year-old self's birthday party and people were speaking about you, what would you want them to say about how you lived? 3. What are three qualities you most admire in others? 4. When do you feel most like yourself? What are you doing, and who are you with? 5. What is one small way you could bring more of what matters to you into the next week? The point of the exercise is not to produce a life plan. It is to remind yourself, in the middle of stress, that the stress is in service of something — and to check whether the way you are currently living is moving toward or away from that something. The answer is often surprising, and the surprise is the value of the exercise. 10.9 A note on meditation apps and programmes Many students access mindfulness through apps — Headspace, Calm, Insight Timer, Smiling Mind, and others. These can be genuinely useful, particularly for beginners who want guided instruction. A few principles: start short (five to ten minutes is enough); be consistent (daily for ten minutes is far more useful than weekly for an hour); do not expect dramatic results (the benefits accumulate over weeks and months, not sessions); and do not force it if a particular app or style does not work for you (there are many approaches; find one that fits). Free alternatives, including the Smiling Mind app and the Palouse Mindfulness free MBSR course, are widely available and as evidence-based as the paid options.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 10.10 When self-care practices are not enough It is worth being honest about the limits of these practices. Mindfulness, selfcompassion, journaling, and breathing are helpful for managing the everyday texture of student stress. They are not sufficient as the only intervention for significant depression or anxiety, for trauma-related conditions, for eating disorders, or for any condition in which professional support is warranted. The student who has been doing all the "right" self-care practices for months and is still struggling is not failing at self-care; they are experiencing something that self-care alone cannot address. Please see Chapter 13 for the broader picture. It is also worth naming a specific risk: self-care can become another thing to fail at. The student who is already overwhelmed and who adds "thirty minutes of meditation, twenty minutes of journaling, and a gratitude practice" to their to-do list has not reduced their load; they have increased it. The practices in this chapter are tools, not obligations. Pick one or two that resonate, use them when they help, and drop the rest. The goal is a lighter life, not a more demanding one. "Self-care is not a checklist. It is a relationship with yourself — one that, like any relationship, takes attention and kindness, not perfection." Chapter 11 turns to a predictable but underappreciated source of student distress: the transitions that punctuate university life, from first year to graduation and beyond.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: CHAPTER 11 Transitions: Starting, Returning, and Finishing Every transition — even a wanted one — is stressful. Knowing that the stress is normal, and that it has a typical shape, makes it easier to bear. SAFETY NOTE This chapter addresses the ordinary stress of academic transitions. If a transition is producing sustained symptoms of depression or anxiety, or if you are returning from a medical or mental-health leave and need support with reintegration, please work with your counselling service and academic advisor. Transitions are the punctuation of student life. They include the obvious ones — starting university, returning after a break, transferring institutions, graduating — and the less obvious ones: starting a new term, moving off campus, beginning a thesis, starting a placement or internship, studying abroad, returning from study abroad, finishing a long-term relationship, the end of a sport or club that has structured your time. Each of these transitions involves loss (of the previous structure, identity, or community) and gain (of the new one), and the brain handles the simultaneous loss and gain clumsily, often producing a dip in mood and a spike in anxiety even when the transition is entirely wanted. This chapter walks through the major transition points of student life and the protective moves that, according to the research and clinical literature, make them easier. 11.1 The first-year transition The transition into university is one of the largest transitions in modern life. It typically involves a new city, new housing, new social network, new academic expectations, new financial responsibilities, new food, new sleep schedule, and a new identity — all happening simultaneously, often within a single week.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: into university is one of the largest transitions in modern life. It typically involves a new city, new housing, new social network, new academic expectations, new financial responsibilities, new food, new sleep schedule, and a new identity — all happening simultaneously, often within a single week. The brain, which handles novelty well in small doses and poorly in avalanches, is confronted with an avalanche. The first six to twelve weeks are, for most students, a period of measurable stress, elevated cortisol, disrupted sleep, and mood volatility — even when the student is enjoying the experience and would not want to be anywhere else.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: The single most useful reframe for first-year students is that the dip is normal. The student who arrives excited and then, three weeks in, finds themselves overwhelmed, lonely, and questioning whether they made the right choice is not failing the transition; they are experiencing it. The dip typically bottoms out around weeks four to eight and gradually lifts over the rest of the first term as friendships form, routines establish, and the environment becomes familiar. Students who know this in advance weather the dip better than students who conclude, at week four, that they are uniquely unsuited to university. PROTECTIVE MOVES FOR FIRST YEAR Build structure early. A regular wake time, a regular class attendance pattern, a regular meal time, a regular study block. Structure reduces cognitive load and supports sleep. Join one recurring activity in the first two weeks. Club, sport, society, volunteer group, part-time job. The specific activity matters less than the recurring contact with the same people. Be honest with people back home about how it is going. The temptation to perform "everything is great" is strong and isolating. Limit major decisions in the first term. Switching programmes, dropping out, ending a long-distance relationship, getting a tattoo — these are decisions better made after the transition dip has lifted, not during it. Use orientation and first-year support programmes. Most universities offer mentoring, first-year seminars, peer support, and academic skills programmes specifically designed to ease the transition. Use them. Know where to seek help before you need it. Find the counselling service, the academic advising office, the financial aid office, and the disability office in the first few weeks, when you do not need them.

text: pport, and academic skills programmes specifically designed to ease the transition. Use them. Know where to seek help before you need it. Find the counselling service, the academic advising office, the financial aid office, and the disability office in the first few weeks, when you do not need them. Knowing where they are makes it easier to go when you do. 11.2 Returning after a break or leave Returning to university after a break — whether a summer, a year abroad, a medical or mental-health leave, or a withdrawal and re-entry — is its own transition, and often a harder one than the initial arrival. The student returning from a leave in particular is often navigating two transitions at once: the return to academic demands, and the re-engagement with whatever circumstances led to

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: the leave. The dip in mood and increase in anxiety that can accompany the return are not signs that the leave failed; they are signs that the return is, itself, a major transition. For students returning from a mental-health leave specifically, the following can help: have a written return plan developed with the counselling service and academic advisor, including reduced load if appropriate, regular check-ins, and a clear set of warning signs that would prompt reaching out for support; resume protective practices before the return — sleep, movement, social contact, therapy appointments — so that they are already established when academic demands resume; communicate with trusted people on campus (an advisor, a friend, a residence advisor) about what you need and what they should look out for; build in more recovery time than you think you need in the first weeks; and be patient — the rhythm of academic life takes a few weeks to feel natural again, and that is normal. 11.3 Transferring institutions Transferring to a new institution combines elements of the first-year transition (new environment, new social network) with elements of returning after a break (already-established academic identity and habits). Transfer students often report feeling "between" cohorts — too experienced for the first-year orientation, too new for the second-year cohort that has already formed social bonds. The protective moves are similar to those for first year: build structure, join recurring activities, be honest with people back home, and know where to seek help. In addition, transfer-specific support groups or mentoring programmes, where they exist, can substantially reduce the sense of being between cohorts.

text: e moves are similar to those for first year: build structure, join recurring activities, be honest with people back home, and know where to seek help. In addition, transfer-specific support groups or mentoring programmes, where they exist, can substantially reduce the sense of being between cohorts. 11.4 Study abroad Studying abroad is, for most students, a positive and developmental experience — but it is also a major transition with predictable stress points. The arrival phase involves culture shock, language adjustment, homesickness, and the logistics of a new city; the middle phase typically involves a peak of enjoyment and engagement as the environment becomes familiar; the departure phase can produce grief at leaving and anxiety about re-entry; and the return home often produces "reverse culture shock" — the disorienting experience of finding home less familiar than expected, and of finding that the people at home have not had the parallel experience you have had.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Protective moves: research and prepare for culture shock before you go; build a local social network early (clubs, classes, host family) rather than relying on calls home; limit calls home in the early weeks to force local engagement; document your experience (photos, journal) to support later integration; and prepare for re-entry before you return — anticipate that home will feel different, that you will have changed, and that the people at home may not fully understand. Many universities offer re-entry workshops for returning studyabroad students; if yours does, attend it. 11.5 International student transitions International students navigate the standard student transitions plus additional layers: visa and immigration stress, language demands, cultural adjustment, financial complexity (often including exchange rates and family expectations across borders), homesickness that is harder to address with a quick visit home, and the experience of being visibly or invisibly "other" in a host culture. The mental-health impact is substantial — international students show higher rates of depression and anxiety than domestic students in most studies, and lower rates of formal help-seeking.

text: to address with a quick visit home, and the experience of being visibly or invisibly "other" in a host culture. The mental-health impact is substantial — international students show higher rates of depression and anxiety than domestic students in most studies, and lower rates of formal help-seeking. Protective moves specific to international students: connect with an international student office or association early; find compatriots (other students from your country) for shared cultural reference and language; build relationships with both compatriots and host-country students, rather than choosing one or the other; understand your visa conditions and where to seek advice if they are threatened; be aware that homesickness is normal and typically eases over the first year; and recognise that the experience of being "other" is a real stressor, not a personal failing to be powered through. Many universities have counselling services with specific expertise in international student issues; please use them. 11.6 The post-graduation transition The transition out of university is, for many students, harder than the transition in — and far less prepared for. The structures that have organised life for three or four years (terms, courses, exams, social networks built around campus) disappear overnight. The next step — job, graduate programme, gap year, return home — is often uncertain. The social network disperses. The identity of "student", which has been central, is suddenly gone. The result, for many recent graduates, is a period of disorientation, anxiety, low mood, and identity confusion that can last for months.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: The post-graduation transition is sometimes called "the post-graduation void" or "quarter-life crisis", and it is far more common than the cultural narrative acknowledges. The student who graduated with a good degree, has a job offer or a plan, and yet feels persistently lost or low in the months after graduation is not failing adult life; they are navigating a transition that the culture underprepares them for. Protective moves: maintain contact with at least some of the university social network; build structure into the post-graduation weeks (a routine, a job search schedule, a fitness routine, a class); be patient with the absence of clear direction; avoid comparing your insides to other graduates' curated outsides; and recognise that the first year after graduation is a transition, not a verdict on the rest of your life. "Transitions are not interruptions of your life. They are your life, in a different shape. Treat them with the respect you would give any major event." 11.7 A general model for navigating transitions Regardless of the specific transition, a few principles apply across the board: Expect a dip. Mood and energy typically dip for four to twelve weeks during a major transition. Knowing this is normal reduces the secondary anxiety of "why am I not fine?" Keep anchors from before. A friendship, a routine, a hobby, a piece of music, a familiar food. Anchors provide continuity while the new environment becomes familiar. Build structure into the new. Regular wake time, regular meals, regular activity. The structure does the work of stabilisation while the brain is processing novelty. Resist the comparison narrative. "Everyone else is fine" is almost always false.

The structure does the work of stabilisation while the brain is processing novelty. Resist the comparison narrative. "Everyone else is fine" is almost always false. The students who appear to be handling the transition effortlessly are, in most cases, managing it less well than they appear. Avoid major decisions during the dip. Transitions can activate underlying vulnerabilities, and early support is more effective than delayed support.

text: Chapter 12 turns to a factor that shapes every transition and every other chapter in this guide: the intersection of identity, culture, and mental health. CHAPTER 12 Identity, Culture, and Mental Health Your identity — race, gender, sexuality, disability, class, immigration status, religion — is not a side variable in your mental health. It shapes every other factor in this guide. SAFETY NOTE This chapter addresses identity-based stress and minority stress in general terms. If you have experienced discrimination, harassment, or hate crimes on campus, please contact your campus equity office, student services, or campus safety. These are not just "stress" — they are events that institutions have a responsibility to address. Mental health is not identity-neutral. The risk factors and protective factors covered in earlier chapters do not operate the same way for all students; they are shaped, often profoundly, by identity. A first-generation student's experience of academic stress is different from a legacy student's. A Black student's experience of campus social life is different from a white student's. A transgender student's experience of campus housing is different from a cisgender student's. A student with a visible disability navigates the campus differently from a student without one. These differences are not soft variables; they are concrete, daily, and they produce measurable effects on mental health. This chapter is necessarily incomplete — a single chapter cannot do justice to the intersection of identity, culture, and mental health.

This chapter is necessarily incomplete — a single chapter cannot do justice to the intersection of identity, culture, and mental health. What it can do is name the major patterns the research literature documents, validate the experiences of students whose identities are often unaddressed in mainstream mental-health discussions, and signpost where to find more specific support. 12.1 Minority stress: the concept The concept of minority stress, developed by the researcher Ilan Meyer in the context of LGBTQ+ mental health, refers to the chronic excess stress experienced by members of stigmatised groups, independent of any single

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: discriminatory event. Minority stress has three components: external stressors (actual experiences of discrimination, violence, rejection); expectation of stress (the vigilance that comes from anticipating further discrimination); and internalised stigma (the absorption of negative cultural messages about one's group). The model has since been applied to racial and ethnic minorities, religious minorities, people with disabilities, and other marginalised groups, and is one of the most useful frameworks for understanding why students from marginalised groups show higher rates of depression and anxiety even in the absence of overt discrimination on a given day. Minority stress is the weather, not the storm. It explains why students from marginalised groups can experience physiological activation — elevated cortisol, disrupted sleep, anxiety — that their peers do not, even on days when nothing obviously bad has happened. The constant low-level vigilance of "will I be misgendered", "will I be tokenised", "will I be followed in the shop", "will my accent be mocked" is itself a stressor, and it accumulates. 12.2 Race, ethnicity, and mental health Students of colour, in predominantly white institutions and in many multicultural institutions, navigate a range of identity-based stressors that white students do not.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: followed in the shop", "will my accent be mocked" is itself a stressor, and it accumulates. 12.2 Race, ethnicity, and mental health Students of colour, in predominantly white institutions and in many multicultural institutions, navigate a range of identity-based stressors that white students do not. These include overt racial discrimination (which remains common on university campuses, despite institutional commitments to the contrary); subtler microaggressions (being asked "where are you really from", being told you are "articulate", being confused with the only other student of your race in the class); the cognitive load of code-switching (adjusting speech, behaviour, hair, clothing, and even name pronunciation to fit dominant norms); the experience of tokenisation (being asked to speak for your race in seminars or on committees); stereotype threat (the well-documented performance decrement that occurs when students fear confirming negative stereotypes about their group); and the isolation of being one of very few students of colour in a programme or residence. The mental-health impact is well-documented: students of colour show higher rates of depression and anxiety, lower rates of formal help-seeking, and higher rates of negative experiences when they do seek help (including misdiagnosis, cultural incompetence, and microaggressions from providers). The protective factors include: connection with same-race peers and mentors; culturally responsive counselling (many universities now have counsellors of colour or partnerships with community organisations); ethnic student associations and

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: cultural centres; involvement in faith communities where relevant; and the development of a strong positive racial identity, which buffers against the impact of external racism. 12.3 Gender and mental health Gender shapes mental health in multiple ways. Women show higher rates of depression and anxiety than men across most studies, partly biological (hormonal factors, including menstrual cycle, contraception, pregnancy, and perimenopause), partly social (higher rates of sexual violence, harassment, unpaid care work, and economic precarity; higher exposure to appearancebased comparison; socialisation toward rumination rather than externalising). Men show lower rates of diagnosed depression and anxiety but higher rates of suicide, substance use, and externalising behaviours — a pattern that reflects, in part, socialisation away from emotional expression and help-seeking, and toward "toughing it out". The result is that men's mental-health problems are often underdiagnosed and undertreated, with serious consequences. Transgender, non-binary, and gender-diverse students show substantially elevated rates of depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicidal ideation — a disparity that is largely attributable to minority stress (discrimination, misgendering, lack of access to gender-affirming care, family rejection, hostile policy environments) rather than to being trans itself. The protective factors are well-documented: use of chosen name and pronouns, access to genderaffirming healthcare, support from family and peers, presence of trans-inclusive policies and facilities on campus, and connection with trans community. Many universities now have dedicated LGBTQ+ centres or services; please use them.

Many universities now have dedicated LGBTQ+ centres or services; please use them. 12.4 Sexuality and mental health LGBTQ+ students, as a group, show higher rates of depression, anxiety, substance use, and suicidal ideation than heterosexual and cisgender peers — a disparity that, as with trans students, is largely attributable to minority stress rather than to sexual orientation itself. The protective factors are similar: family acceptance, peer support, presence of affirming communities and faith traditions, access to LGBTQ+competent healthcare, and institutional policies and services that are visibly inclusive. The single most important protective factor for many LGBTQ+ students is having at least one trusted adult to whom they are out — a parent, teacher, mentor, or counsellor. If you are not yet out to anyone, please consider reaching out to an LGBTQ+ helpline or campus service as a first step; you do not have to do it alone.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 12.5 Disability and mental health Students with disabilities — physical, sensory, cognitive, developmental, or psychiatric — navigate a campus environment that is often not designed for them, despite legal mandates for accessibility. The mental-health impact is substantial: chronic illness and disability are associated with higher rates of depression and anxiety (partly through the biological effects of some conditions, partly through the social and structural barriers students encounter); students with psychiatric disabilities often face compounded stigma; and students with invisible disabilities (including ADHD, autism, learning disabilities, and chronic illness) often face scepticism about the legitimacy of their needs. Protective factors: register with the disability office early, even if you are not sure you need accommodations — having the relationship established makes it easier to access support when you do; know your rights under relevant disability law (the ADA in the US, the Equality Act in the UK, equivalent laws elsewhere); find disability community on campus or online, which can be a powerful counter to isolation; work with clinicians who understand your specific condition; and do not internalise the message that needing accommodation is "less than" — accommodation is a right, not a favour. 12.6 First-generation students First-generation students — those whose parents did not attend university — face a specific set of stressors that are often invisible to continuing-generation peers and to the institution itself.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: ng accommodation is "less than" — accommodation is a right, not a favour. 12.6 First-generation students First-generation students — those whose parents did not attend university — face a specific set of stressors that are often invisible to continuing-generation peers and to the institution itself. These include structural unfamiliarity (not knowing the unwritten rules of academic life — how to talk to professors, what office hours are for, how to choose a major, what "networking" means, how to apply for internships); financial precarity (first-generation students are more likely to be working long hours, to be food insecure, and to lack family financial backup); family dynamics (families may be proud but unfamiliar with the demands of university life, may have expectations about contribution to the household, may not understand why their student is "still studying" rather than earning); cultural mismatch between home and university environments; and imposter feelings — the persistent sense of not belonging, of having got in by mistake, of being found out. Protective factors: first-generation student programmes (many universities now have these); mentoring by first-generation faculty or upper-year students; explicit education about the unwritten rules; financial support targeted at firstgeneration students; and reframing the imposter feelings as a normal response to being in a new environment, not a verdict on your capacity. First-generation

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: students who graduate do so at rates comparable to continuing-generation students when they have access to appropriate support; the gap is in support, not in capacity. 12.7 Class and socioeconomic background Class operates as a background variable that shapes almost every other factor in this guide. Students from low-income backgrounds face financial stress, food insecurity, work obligations, housing precarity, and the cognitive load of managing trade-offs that wealthier peers do not face. They also face subtle cultural mismatches: the assumption of having travelled, of having certain forms of cultural capital, of having family networks that include professionals, of having "backup options" if a programme does not work out. These mismatches produce a particular kind of exhaustion — the constant low-grade work of translating between the academic environment and the home environment — that is itself a stressor. The protective factors for class-based stress overlap heavily with those for firstgeneration students, and include financial support, mentoring, community with other low-income students, and the reframing of class background as a source of resilience and perspective rather than a deficit. Many universities have specific programmes for low-income students; if yours does, please use it. 12.8 International students and acculturative stress International students were addressed in Chapter 11 in the context of transitions. From an identity perspective, they also navigate acculturative stress — the stress of adapting to a new cultural environment while maintaining connection to the culture of origin.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: nal students and acculturative stress International students were addressed in Chapter 11 in the context of transitions. From an identity perspective, they also navigate acculturative stress — the stress of adapting to a new cultural environment while maintaining connection to the culture of origin. The patterns of adaptation vary: some students assimilate quickly into the host culture, sometimes at the cost of disconnection from their culture of origin; some remain primarily within their compatriot community, sometimes at the cost of slower language acquisition and host-culture integration; some integrate both, maintaining strong ties to both cultures; and some experience marginalisation in both. The integration pattern is generally associated with the best mental-health outcomes, but the right pattern for any individual student depends on their specific circumstances and preferences. 12.9 Religious and spiritual identity For students whose religious or spiritual identity is central, that identity can be a substantial source of meaning, community, and resilience — and, in some contexts, a source of stress. The stress arises from several sources: religious

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: discrimination (which affects Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Sikh, and other religiousminority students in different ways in different contexts); conflicts between religious teachings and other aspects of identity (particularly around sexuality and gender, where religious and LGBTQ+ identities can be experienced as in tension, sometimes producing profound internal conflict); cultural mismatch between religious norms and campus norms (around alcohol, dating, dress, food); and spiritual crisis — periods of doubt, questioning, or loss of faith that can be disorienting, particularly for students whose faith has been central to their identity and community. Protective factors include: connection with a religious or spiritual community on or near campus; chaplaincy or multi-faith services, which most universities offer and which can provide support that is not exclusively religious; access to religiously literate mental-health providers (many counselling services can refer to faith-sensitive therapists); and, for students experiencing conflict between religious and other identities, support from communities that have navigated similar tensions (such as LGBTQ+ affirming faith communities, which exist within most major religious traditions). 12.10 Intersectionality: why single-axis framings fail The categories above are not independent. A student who is Black, queer, firstgeneration, and low-income is not experiencing four separate stressors; they are experiencing a single, interlocking system of stressors that shape every aspect of their university life. The concept of intersectionality, developed by the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, names this reality: identity categories intersect in ways that produce experiences not captured by any single category.

The concept of intersectionality, developed by the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, names this reality: identity categories intersect in ways that produce experiences not captured by any single category. A Black woman's experience of campus is not the sum of "Black student" and "woman student"; it is its own specific experience, with its own specific stressors and protective factors. The same is true for every intersectional position. The practical implication for this guide is that the recommendations here are starting points, not complete pictures. Each student's specific situation is shaped by their specific set of identities and contexts, and the most useful support often comes from communities and providers who share or are trained in those specific intersections. Please seek out such support where it exists, and please advocate for its existence where it does not.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 12.11 Finding culturally responsive support Not all counselling is equally helpful for all students. A counsellor who does not understand the role of family in your culture, the specific history of your community, the meaning of your religious practices, or the lived reality of your disability may, even with the best intentions, provide support that misses the mark. The following strategies can help you find support that fits: Ask explicitly when contacting a counselling service whether they have counsellors from your background or with specific experience working with your community. Most services will be transparent about this. Use community-specific resources where they exist: Black, Asian, Latine, LGBTQ+, Muslim, Jewish, and many other communities have mental-health organisations that provide or refer to culturally responsive care. Consider online counselling if local options are not a fit — services like Therapy for Black Girls, the Trevor Project, Identity LGBTQ+ support, and many culturally specific platforms now exist. Use peer support from students who share your identity, through student associations, mentoring programmes, or peer-support groups. Peer support is not a substitute for clinical care when needed, but it is a powerful protective factor in its own right. Advocate for yourself if a provider is not a fit. A first appointment that does not feel right is information, not a verdict. You are allowed to switch providers, ask for a referral, or seek care elsewhere. "Your identity is not a complication to be worked around. It is the lens through which you experience everything else.

Chapter 13 turns to one of the most important and most delayed decisions in student mental health: when and how to seek professional support.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: CHAPTER 13 Recognising When Self-Care Is Not Enough Self-care is necessary but not sufficient. Knowing when to add professional support is itself a protective skill — and one most students delay for far too long. SAFETY NOTE This chapter helps you recognise when to seek professional support. It is not a diagnostic tool. If you are in immediate danger to yourself or someone else, please skip to Chapter 15 and contact emergency services or a crisis line now. Most student mental-health struggles are manageable with the protective practices covered in earlier chapters — sleep, social connection, movement, study habits, and the coping skills of Chapter 10. But not all of them. Some struggles cross a line that self-care alone cannot address, and recognising that line is one of the most important skills in this guide. Students who recognise it early and seek appropriate support tend to recover faster, more completely, and with less disruption to their academic and social lives than students who delay. Students who delay often do so for understandable reasons — stigma, cost, uncertainty about what to expect, hope that things will improve on their own — but the delay usually makes the eventual recovery harder, not easier. This chapter aims to demystify the process. It walks through how to tell when ordinary distress has crossed into something that warrants professional support, what "elevated screening risk" actually means, what to expect from a first counselling appointment, how to overcome the common barriers to seeking help, and how to integrate professional support with the self-care practices covered elsewhere in this guide. 13.1 The line between ordinary distress and something more Distress is normal.

Depression and anxiety, in the clinical sense, are not just "more distress" — they are patterns of distress that have become persistent, pervasive, and disabling. The following questions can help you tell the difference. None of them, alone, is diagnostic; but if several resonate, it is worth taking seriously.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: A SELF-REFLECTION (NOT A DIAGNOSTIC TOOL) Consider the last two weeks. Have you experienced the following? 1. Low mood, sadness, or emptiness on most days, for most of the day, for two weeks or more? ☐ Yes ☐ No 2. Loss of interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy, on most days? ☐ Yes ☐ No 3. Significant changes in sleep (much more or much less than usual) lasting two weeks or more? ☐ Yes ☐ No 4. Significant changes in appetite or weight? ☐ Yes ☐ No 5. Persistent fatigue or loss of energy, even after rest? ☐ Yes ☐ No 6. Difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions that is affecting your daily life? ☐ Yes ☐ No 7. Persistent feelings of worthlessness, guilt, or self-blame? ☐ Yes ☐ No 8. Recurrent thoughts of death, dying, or not wanting to be here? ☐ Yes ☐ No (If yes, please see Chapter 15 immediately.) 9. Excessive worry or anxiety that is difficult to control, on most days, for six months or more? ☐ Yes ☐ No 10. Restlessness, feeling on edge, or difficulty relaxing? ☐ Yes ☐ No 11. Panic attacks — sudden episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms like racing heart, shortness of breath, dizziness? ☐ Yes ☐ No 12. Avoidance of situations because of anxiety (classes, social events, public spaces)? ☐ Yes ☐ No 13. Distress that is interfering with your ability to study, work, socialise, or care for yourself? ☐ Yes ☐ No 14. Increased use of alcohol, cannabis, or other substances to cope? ☐ Yes ☐ No 15. Withdrawal from friends, family, or activities that previously mattered to you? ☐ Yes ☐ No If you answered "yes" to several of these — particularly if the experiences have lasted two weeks or more and are interfering with your daily life — please consider reaching out to a professional. This is not a diagnosis.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 13.2 What "elevated screening risk" actually means You may have encountered the phrase "elevated screening risk" through a screening questionnaire at your university health service, through an online screening tool, or in materials associated with this guide. The phrase sounds clinical, but it is important to understand what it does and does not mean. A screening questionnaire — typically the PHQ-9 for depression or the GAD-7 for anxiety — asks about the frequency of symptoms over the past two weeks. The score provides a rough indication of the likelihood that you are currently experiencing a clinically significant condition. A score in the "elevated" range does not mean you have a diagnosis. It means that, statistically, a substantial proportion of people with that score do meet criteria for a diagnosis, and that follow-up with a qualified professional is recommended. It is the mental-health equivalent of a smoke alarm going off: worth investigating, not worth panicking about, and definitely not worth ignoring. What elevated screening risk does not mean: that you are broken, that you must start treatment, that you are dangerous, that you will be labelled, that the information will go on your permanent record (it will not — health information is confidential), or that you have failed at self-care. It is information, and the appropriate response to the information is to talk to someone qualified to interpret it and to help you figure out what, if anything, to do next. A USEFUL REFRAME A screening score is not a verdict. It is a piece of data, like a temperature reading. A high temperature does not tell you what illness you have or what to do about it; it tells you that something is worth paying attention to. A high screening score does the same.

A high temperature does not tell you what illness you have or what to do about it; it tells you that something is worth paying attention to. A high screening score does the same. The clinician you speak with will help you make sense of it in the context of your specific life. 13.3 What to expect from a first counselling appointment One of the biggest barriers to seeking help is not knowing what will happen when you do. The reality, at most university counselling services, is more mundane and less intimidating than the fear. A first appointment — sometimes called an intake, an assessment, or an initial consultation — typically lasts thirty to sixty minutes and follows a roughly predictable structure. The counsellor will ask about what brought you in. This is your chance to describe, in your own words, what has been going on. You do not need to have prepared a perfect narrative; you can simply describe your experiences, in

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: whatever order makes sense to you. The counsellor may ask clarifying questions — about when the difficulties started, what makes them better or worse, what you have tried so far, what your life looks like more broadly (sleep, social, academic, family, substance use). They may ask about your history — previous mental-health experiences, family history, significant life events. They may ask some standardised questions, often using the same screening tools you may have taken online. They may ask about safety — whether you have had thoughts of suicide or self-harm, and if so, whether you have any plans or intent. These questions are routine, not alarmist; please answer honestly. The counsellor will then typically discuss with you what they are hearing, what options are available, and what they would recommend. Options may include: brief individual counselling at the service (often six to twelve sessions, free at most universities); referral to a longer-term or specialised service outside the university; group therapy or psychoeducational groups; psychiatric consultation (for medication evaluation, if relevant); referral to other campus services (academic advising, disability services, financial aid); or, if what you are experiencing is within the normal range of student distress, validation and discussion of self-care strategies. You are not obligated to accept any particular recommendation. The appointment is a conversation, not a contract. You can ask questions, express preferences, request a different type of support, or take time to think about it. The counsellor's job is to help you figure out what would be most helpful for you, not to impose a plan.

You can ask questions, express preferences, request a different type of support, or take time to think about it. The counsellor's job is to help you figure out what would be most helpful for you, not to impose a plan. 13.4 How to make the first appointment The mechanics of making an appointment vary by institution, but the general process is similar. Most university counselling services accept self-referral — you do not need a doctor's referral or a diagnosis to access them. You typically contact the service by phone, email, or online form, briefly describe that you would like to talk to someone, and they will offer you an initial appointment. Wait times vary; in periods of high demand, you may wait a week or two for an initial appointment, though most services have provisions for urgent same-day or next-day appointments if you are in crisis. Many students find the act of making the appointment harder than the appointment itself. The following can help: write down what you want to say when you call or email, even if it is just "I have been struggling with my mental health and would like to make an appointment to talk to someone"; ask a friend to sit with you or make the call for you if you cannot face it alone; use email or

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: an online form if phone calls are too anxiety-provoking; and do not minimise what you are experiencing — saying "I am fine, I just want to talk" may result in a lower-priority appointment than saying "I have been feeling depressed and it is affecting my classes". IF THE FIRST APPOINTMENT IS NOT A FIT Not every counsellor is a fit for every student. The first appointment may feel unhelpful for many reasons — a mismatch of style, a lack of cultural understanding, a sense of not being heard. This is normal and not a verdict on you or on counselling in general. You are allowed to request a different counsellor, to ask for a different approach, or to seek a different service. Most counselling services expect this and will support you in finding the right fit. Please do not conclude from one unhelpful appointment that no support will help you. 13.5 Common barriers (and how to address them) "I AM NOT BAD ENOUGH TO NEED HELP." You do not need to be at a crisis point to benefit from support. Most counselling services expect to see students with a wide range of concerns, including ordinary stress, relationship difficulties, identity questions, and adjustment problems. If what you are experiencing is bothering you and you would like to talk to someone, that is sufficient reason to make an appointment. Waiting until you are "bad enough" usually means waiting until the problem is harder to address. "I SHOULD BE ABLE TO HANDLE THIS ON MY OWN." There is a cultural narrative, particularly strong in some communities and around masculinity, that seeking help is a sign of weakness. The evidence is the opposite.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: until you are "bad enough" usually means waiting until the problem is harder to address. "I SHOULD BE ABLE TO HANDLE THIS ON MY OWN." There is a cultural narrative, particularly strong in some communities and around masculinity, that seeking help is a sign of weakness. The evidence is the opposite. Students who seek appropriate support are using available resources to address a problem — which is the same skill involved in using a textbook to learn a subject, or seeing a doctor for a physical health concern. The narrative that mental health should be handled alone is itself a risk factor for worse outcomes. "WHAT WILL GO ON MY RECORD?" Health information, including mental-health information, is confidential. Counselling records are not part of your academic transcript. Employers and graduate programmes do not have access to them. The exceptions are narrow

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: — typically involving imminent risk to yourself or others, child or elder abuse, or court orders — and your counsellor would discuss any necessary disclosure with you. Confidentiality is a legal and ethical requirement, not a courtesy. "I CANNOT AFFORD IT." Most university counselling services are free to enrolled students. If you need longer-term or specialised care that the university cannot provide, the counselling service can usually refer you to low-cost community options, sliding-scale clinics, or services covered by your health insurance. If cost is a barrier, please say so; the people whose job it is to help you have encountered this before and have options. "I AM FROM A CULTURE WHERE THIS IS NOT DONE." Many cultures have strong norms against discussing personal problems with strangers, particularly mental-health problems. These norms are real and worth respecting. They are also, in many cases, contributing to higher rates of unaddressed mental-health problems in those communities. If formal counselling is not acceptable to you, please consider alternative forms of support: a religious leader, an elder, a family friend, a community organisation, a peer-support group, or a culturally specific mental-health service. The form of support matters less than the act of letting someone in. "I TRIED IT BEFORE AND IT DID NOT HELP." This is a real and discouraging experience, and it is more common than the counselling field often acknowledges. There are several reasons counselling may not have helped in the past: it was the wrong type of therapy for your concern; the therapist was not a fit; the timing was wrong; the number of sessions was too few; or your circumstances at the time made it difficult to engage. None of these mean that no support will help.

None of these mean that no support will help. Please consider trying again, ideally with a different type of therapy or a different provider. Many students who did not benefit from counselling the first time benefit substantially the second. "I DO NOT HAVE TIME." Time is a real constraint, and adding a weekly appointment to an already overloaded schedule is genuinely difficult. The counter-consideration is that untreated mental-health problems typically consume more time — through procrastination, lost productivity, missed classes, and the cognitive load of struggling — than the appointment would. A fifty-minute weekly appointment that allows you to function better in the rest of your week is a net time gain, not a loss.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 13.6 Integrating professional support with self-care Professional support and self-care are not alternatives; they are complements. The student who is in counselling and also sleeping adequately, moving regularly, maintaining social connection, and using the coping skills of Chapter 10 will typically progress faster than the student who is in counselling but neglecting the rest. Conversely, the student who is using self-care well but is still struggling will typically benefit from adding professional support rather than from "trying harder" at self-care. The two also inform each other. The insights you gain in counselling — about your patterns, your history, your triggers — can sharpen the way you use selfcare practices. The observations you make in self-care — what makes you better or worse, what you have tried, what has worked — can give your counsellor valuable material to work with. Please do not treat them as separate domains; treat them as two halves of a single project. 13.7 A note on medication This guide does not provide medication information, and medication decisions are made with a clinician, not a book. What this guide can say is that psychiatric medication, where it is appropriate, is one tool among several, that it is often combined with therapy rather than replacing it, that decisions about starting, changing, or stopping medication should be made with a prescriber rather than independently, and that stigma about medication is widespread but largely unjustified. If a clinician recommends medication as part of your care, please consider the recommendation on its merits, ask questions, and make an informed decision — rather than dismissing it out of hand based on cultural or personal narratives about medication.

text: dication is widespread but largely unjustified. If a clinician recommends medication as part of your care, please consider the recommendation on its merits, ask questions, and make an informed decision — rather than dismissing it out of hand based on cultural or personal narratives about medication. 13.8 A final note: relapse is not failure Mental-health recovery is rarely linear. Most students who recover from depression or anxiety experience periods of improvement followed by periods of setback, sometimes over months or years. A setback is not a failure of treatment or of self-care; it is part of the natural course of these conditions. The useful response to a setback is to recognise it early, reach out to your existing support, and adjust — not to conclude that "nothing works" and disengage. The students who recover most fully are typically not those who never relapse; they are those who learn to recognise early warning signs, respond to them, and return to the practices and supports that helped before.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: "Asking for help is not the alternative to being strong. It is one of the ways strong people stay strong." Chapter 14 turns to the parallel question: what to do when it is not you who is struggling, but a friend. CHAPTER 14 Supporting a Friend When someone you care about is struggling, you want to help. The good news is that you can — often more than you think. The boundary to remember is that you are a friend, not a therapist. SAFETY NOTE This chapter offers guidance on supporting a friend through ordinary distress. If a friend is in immediate danger to themselves or others, do not try to handle it alone — contact emergency services, campus safety, or a crisis line (see Chapter 15). A friend in crisis needs more than a friend can provide. Friends are often the first to notice when a student is struggling — before the student themselves, before family, and long before any professional. The role of a friend in mental health is genuinely powerful: you are often the person who validates the experience, who reduces the isolation, who suggests seeking help, who stays connected when the student withdraws. Research on help-seeking consistently finds that the single most influential factor in a student's decision to seek professional support is the encouragement of a trusted friend. You matter more than you think. That said, the role has limits. You are not trained to assess risk, to provide therapy, or to manage a crisis. Trying to play those roles — however lovingly — can harm both your friend and yourself. This chapter is about how to be a good friend in the spaces where friendship helps, and how to recognise and respect the boundaries where professional support is needed.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 14.1 Noticing the signs The signs that a friend is struggling are often subtle and accumulate gradually. They include: Withdrawal — pulling back from social activities, taking longer to reply to messages, skipping classes or commitments they previously attended. Mood changes — seeming flatter, more irritable, more anxious, or more hopeless than usual. A friend who used to laugh easily and now rarely does. Behavioural changes — changes in sleep (looking exhausted, sleeping at odd hours), appetite (weight loss or gain), substance use (drinking more, alone, or at unusual times), self-care (skipping showers, wearing the same clothes repeatedly). Academic changes — missing deadlines, skipping classes, dropping activities, talking about giving up or dropping out. Conversation changes — talking more about hopelessness, being a burden, feeling trapped; or, conversely, going quiet about how they are doing. Social media changes — posting noticeably more or less, posting darker content, posting about feeling hopeless or wanting to disappear. Direct statements — talking about death, dying, suicide, or "not being here". These should always be taken seriously (see below). None of these signs, in isolation, means a friend is in crisis. But if several show up together and persist for more than a couple of weeks, it is worth reaching out. The act of reaching out — of showing that someone has noticed — is itself often a relief to the person struggling. 14.2 Starting the conversation Many people avoid starting the conversation because they do not know what to say. The good news is that the specific words matter less than the act of showing up. The following structure, adapted from mental-health first aid training, can help:

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: A SIMPLE SCRIPT 1. Name what you have noticed, specifically and without judgment. "Hey, I have noticed you have been quieter than usual the last couple of weeks, and you missed a few classes. I just wanted to check in." 2. Express care, not alarm. "I am not trying to make a big deal of it. I just wanted you to know I have noticed, and I care about how you are doing." 3. Ask openly, and give them room to answer or not. "How are you doing, actually? And it is okay if you do not want to talk about it right now." 4. Listen more than you talk. Do not rush to fix, advise, or minimise. Let them tell you what is going on, in their own words. 5. Ask what would be helpful. "Is there anything I can do that would help right now? Even just listening, or helping you find someone to talk to?" 6. Follow up. One conversation rarely resolves anything. The consistency of checking in — a text a few days later, an invitation to coffee next week — matters more than the eloquence of any single exchange. 14.3 What to say (and not say) Certain responses, while well-intentioned, tend to shut down rather than open up conversation. The following contrast may be useful.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: OFTEN UNHELPFUL OFTEN MORE HELPFUL "You have so much to live for." "I am glad you are here. I care about you." "Other people have it much worse." "That sounds really hard. I am sorry you are going through it." "You should just exercise / sleep more / think positive." "Have you been able to do anything that helps, even a little?" "I know exactly how you feel." "I do not know exactly what this is like for you, but I want to try to understand." "It will get better." "I am here, and I will keep being here." "You need to see a therapist." "Have you thought about talking to someone at the counselling service? I could go with you if that would help." "Promise me you will not do anything stupid." "I am worried about you. Can we talk about what is going on, and whether you are safe right now?" The general principle: listening, validating, and staying present is almost always more helpful than advising, minimising, or fixing. Your friend does not need you to have answers. They need to know they are not alone. 14.4 When to involve someone else There are situations where being a good friend means involving someone with more training or authority than you have. These include: Direct statements about suicide or self-harm. If a friend talks about wanting to die, about a plan to harm themselves, or about feeling like a burden whose absence would be a relief, take it seriously. Ask directly: "Are you thinking about suicide?" (Research shows this does not increase risk; it reduces it, by opening the conversation.) If they say yes, or if you are seriously concerned, do not leave them alone. Contact a crisis line, campus safety, or emergency services. You can offer to be with them while they call, or to call on their behalf. Severe withdrawal or self-neglect.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide

You can offer to be with them while they call, or to call on their behalf. Severe withdrawal or self-neglect. If a friend has stopped attending classes, stopped eating, stopped leaving their room, or is showing signs of severe self-neglect, the situation has moved beyond what friendship alone can address. Contact a residence advisor, the dean of students, or the counselling service. Acute intoxication or substance overdose. If a friend is in immediate medical danger from alcohol or other substances, call emergency services.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Do not wait to see if they "sleep it off". Evidence of abuse or assault. If a friend discloses abuse (current or past), assault, or harassment, believe them, support them in seeking appropriate help (campus safety,Title IX office, local police, sexual-assault service), and respect their decisions about what to do. Do not pressure them to report if they do not want to. When you are out of your depth. If you are unsure whether a situation is serious, it is okay to consult a residence advisor, counsellor, or helpline yourself, without naming the friend, to get advice on what to do. THE PROMISE OF CONFIDENTIALITY Friendship involves trust, and a friend who is struggling may share things they do not want shared. Take that trust seriously — but understand its limits. Do not promise blanket confidentiality in advance. If a friend asks you to promise not to tell anyone, a reasonable response is: "I will respect your privacy as much as I can, but if I am seriously worried about your safety, I might need to tell someone who can help. I would rather be honest with you about that now than break a promise later." A friend in genuine danger needs more than your silence; they need the help you cannot provide. 14.5 Your own well-being as a supporter Supporting a friend who is struggling takes a real toll. Students who take on significant caring roles for friends in distress often show measurable increases in their own stress, sleep disruption, and academic difficulty. The role is worthwhile; it is also costly, and the cost needs to be acknowledged and managed.

The role is worthwhile; it is also costly, and the cost needs to be acknowledged and managed. Protective practices for supporters include: maintaining your own life — your studies, your sleep, your social connections, your recovery — not as selfishness but as the precondition for being able to help; being clear with your friend about what you can and cannot do — "I am always here to listen, but I cannot be your therapist, and there are people trained for that"; seeking your own support — talking to a counsellor about the impact of supporting a friend is a legitimate and common use of counselling services; taking breaks — you are allowed to step back, particularly if the situation is escalating or if your own wellbeing is suffering; and recognising that you cannot save anyone — you can support, accompany, encourage, and connect, but you cannot do the work of recovery for another person. Their recovery is theirs, not yours.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: "You cannot be the only support a struggling friend has. The most loving thing you can do is help them build a wider net." Chapter 15 addresses the situation every other chapter has been carefully avoiding: what to do when there is a crisis. CHAPTER 15 Crisis Awareness and Emergency Resources This chapter is here for the moments when everything else in this guide is not enough. It does not teach you to be a crisis worker. It signposts where crisis workers can be found. IF YOU ARE IN IMMEDIATE DANGER TO YOURSELF OR SOMEONE ELSE, PLEASE STOP READING THIS GUIDE AND CONTACT EMERGENCY SERVICES NOW. In most of Europe and many other regions, the emergency number is 112. In the US and Canada, it is 911. In the UK, 999. In Australia, 000. If you cannot find your local emergency number, contact your campus security office or any available helpline listed below. A crisis, in the mental-health sense, is a situation in which a person's safety is at acute risk — usually through their own actions, sometimes through the actions of others. This guide is not a crisis-intervention manual. Crisis intervention is a specialised skill that requires training, and attempting it without training can harm both the person in crisis and the person trying to help. What this guide can do is help you recognise when a situation has crossed into crisis, signpost the resources that exist to respond, and offer some basic guidance on what to do — and what not to do — while waiting for help to arrive. If you are reading this chapter because you are worried about yourself, please know that the experience you are having — however overwhelming, however hopeless it feels — is one that other people have had and survived, and that the right help can make a real difference.

The fact that you are still reading is itself a sign that some part of you is reaching for help. Please honour that part by contacting one of the resources below, now, before you do anything else.

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: 15.1 What counts as a crisis? A mental-health crisis can take many forms. The following are situations in which immediate professional help is warranted: Thoughts of suicide with a plan or intent. Thinking about how you would do it, having the means to do it, intending to do it soon. Self-harm that has caused or may cause serious injury. A suicide attempt. If you have taken an overdose, injured yourself, or attempted suicide, please seek medical help immediately, even if you are having second thoughts. Some overdoses cause delayed damage that is not immediately apparent. Acute psychosis — hallucinations, delusions, or loss of contact with reality, particularly if the experience is frightening or involves commands to harm yourself or others. Severe self-neglect — not eating or drinking for days, not sleeping for days, inability to care for basic needs. Acute intoxication with suicidal or violent ideation. Being a danger to others. Being the victim of abuse, assault, or exploitation and needing immediate safety. Being unable to keep yourself safe for any other reason. If any of these apply to you, please contact one of the resources below now. If any of these apply to a friend, please stay with them (in person or on the phone) and contact help on their behalf if they cannot or will not. 15.2 International crisis lines Crisis lines are staffed by trained volunteers or professionals who can listen, support, assess risk, and connect you to local emergency services if needed. Most are free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day. The following list is not exhaustive but covers many countries. If your country is not listed, please search online for "crisis line [your country]" or contact your local emergency services.

If you cannot reach a service, try your local emergency number or your university's campus security. 15.3 What to do while waiting for help If you or someone else is in crisis and you have called for help, the following practices can help keep the situation as safe as possible while you wait. IF YOU ARE IN CRISIS YOURSELF Put distance between yourself and any means of harm. If you are thinking about overdose, move medications out of reach. If you are thinking about a weapon, move away from it. The few seconds of friction often allow the crisis to pass. Do not be alone. If possible, go to a public place, call a friend, or stay on the phone with a crisis line until help arrives. Avoid alcohol and other substances. They lower inhibitions and increase impulsivity, which is the opposite of what you need right now. Do something physical and grounding. A cold shower, a walk outside, holding an ice cube, the breathing practices from Chapter 10. Anything that brings you back into your body and the present moment. Remember that this state will pass. Acute suicidal crises are typically timelimited — the intense urge often lifts within hours, even when the underlying distress persists. Your job right now is to stay safe through the peak of the wave. IF YOU ARE WITH A FRIEND IN CRISIS Stay with them. Do not leave them alone. If you cannot be physically present, stay on the phone. Remove means of harm if it is safe to do so — medications, weapons, ligature points.

If you cannot be physically present, stay on the phone. Remove means of harm if it is safe to do so — medications, weapons, ligature points. Listen without judging, arguing, or minimising. Do not debate whether their life is worth living. Do not tell them to think of their family. Do say: "I am here. I am not leaving. Help is coming."

title: Student Wellbeing Guide
text: Ask directly about suicide. "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" Asking does not increase risk; it often reduces it by opening the conversation. Call for help. Crisis line, emergency services, campus security. You do not need their permission if they are at imminent risk. Do not promise confidentiality. A life is more important than a promise. Take care of yourself afterwards. Being with someone in crisis is traumatic. Please seek your own support — a friend, a counsellor, a crisis line for supporters. 15.4 What happens when you call emergency services Many students hesitate to call emergency services because they do not know what will happen. The reality varies by country and circumstance, but the general pattern is: a trained dispatcher will ask you questions to assess the situation; they may send an ambulance, police, or a crisis-response team; the responding professionals will assess the person in crisis and decide on the appropriate next step, which may include transport to an emergency department, a crisis assessment, or referral to community services. The goal is safety and stabilisation, not punishment or permanent institutionalisation. In most jurisdictions, you cannot be forced into long-term treatment against your will unless you are assessed as lacking capacity to make decisions about your own safety at that moment. Short-term holds (typically 24 to 72 hours) for assessment are possible in some jurisdictions if there is imminent risk. The threshold for these is high and the process is reviewed. The cultural image of "being locked up for being suicidal" is largely outdated and exaggerated; modern crisis care emphasises the least restrictive intervention that keeps you safe.
